#9532. REA: The Open-Source AI Tool That Can Reverse Engineer Almost Anything (2026 Guide)

What if you could ask your AI assistant how any app works and get a real answer, backed by evidence, without ever seeing the source code?

You use an app, tap a feature, and wonder how it was built. Maybe it is a fast search bar, a clever clipboard trick, or a mechanic in an old game. Until recently, finding out meant months of learning disassemblers and reading assembly code. A new open-source project called REA changes that. It has earned more than 430,000 stars on GitHub, and in this guide I will explain what it does, which problems it solves, and how you can start using it today.

Reverse engineering is the practice of studying finished software to understand how it works. It is powerful, but it has never been beginner-friendly. If you have tried it, or even thought about trying it, you have probably run into these obstacles.

Reading assembly code and pseudocode takes a long time to learn. Many curious developers give up before they get their first useful result.

An Electron app needs one approach. An Android APK needs another. A .NET assembly, a native binary, and a website each have their own tools, file formats, and tricks.

Even experts can spend hours following one function through strings, calls, and references just to understand a single small feature.

If you ask a general chatbot how an app works, it may give a confident answer that is simply invented. Without evidence, you cannot tell what is real.

Connecting analysis tools to an AI agent usually requires custom scripts and configuration, and it is easy to break.

REA is a free, MIT-licensed project that connects your AI agent to professional reverse engineering tools through MCP (Model Context Protocol). MCP is a standard way for AI agents to use external tools. In simple terms, REA acts as a bridge between your agent and the software you want to understand. Here is how it answers each problem above.

You do not need the app’s source code. You point your agent at the app, ask a question, and REA helps it trace the answer.

The same workflows are available from the terminal, so you can also script them without an agent. Analysis runs locally on your machine. Your agent receives the tool results, and your AI provider’s own data policy applies to that part.

The range of supported targets is one of REA’s biggest strengths. These are the main groups.

REA returns pseudocode, assembly, strings, symbols, calls, and references. Deep native analysis uses an engine you already have, such as Hopper, Ghidra, IDA, or Kuna. It also supports GNU objdump and Rizin for offline inspection.

This is the easiest place to start, because static JavaScript analysis needs no native engine. REA recovers modules, imports, source maps, routes, IPC connections, and native add-on relationships.

REA can inspect APK manifests, classes, decompiled methods, signatures, and resources. Through adb, it can also look at packages, processes, and logs on an emulator or a real phone. Flutter apps and JEB projects are supported too.

For .NET assemblies, REA reads metadata, CIL instructions, and native dependencies without running the program.

REA can inspect page structure, scripts, and network activity using a Chrome-family browser. It can also read saved HAR and Fiddler SAZ files to examine requests, responses, and exposed payloads.

The list continues with Go and Rust binaries, GPU code objects, GGUF and safetensors model files, Unity IL2CPP metadata, Godot PCK archives, PE imports and certificates, ELF notes, Linux kernel modules, WebAssembly, EVM bytecode, SQLite databases, firmware images, packet captures, and PyInstaller executables. Most of these use built-in static inspection, so no extra software is required.

The project publishes several case studies on its website.

REA can record a web app session and turn its API calls into tools an AI agent can use. It then exports a runnable environment for reinforcement learning or for testing how well an agent completes tasks. With a saved HAR file, the command looks like this:

You then run the result with AgentEnv and Docker, and add your own tasks and reward checks.

You need Node.js and npm. The project lists supported Node versions as 22.x (22.23.4 or newer), 24.x (24.22.1 or newer), or 26.12.1 and above.

Setup supports Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, Grok Build, and other agents. It shows you the proposed changes first and keeps backups of your existing configuration.

The new MCP server is loaded when the agent starts again.

You can inspect an extracted Electron app or ASAR file directly:

To keep REA installed, run npm install --global rea-agents. REA changes quickly, so use rea update to stay current. Updating is also the first fix to try if you run into a bug.

REA combines the reach of dozens of analysis tools with the convenience of an AI agent. It helps you understand software you do not have source code for, and it backs each conclusion with evidence instead of guesses. The range of supported formats, from native binaries to Electron apps to Android devices, is unusually broad for a free tool.

Developers, security researchers, students, software preservationists, and anyone who wants to understand how an app works.

Use REA only on software you own or are authorized to examine.

The project is intended for lawful research, education, interoperability, software preservation, and analysis of software you have permission to study. It does not permit cracked tools, stolen license keys, or bypassing license restrictions. Read the project’s disclaimer before you start.

Also be careful where you download it from. The project warns that a similar repository name or a copied README does not make a download official. Use only these sources:

Only for deep native binary analysis. JavaScript and .NET inspection work without a native engine, and setup can install Hopper with your approval.

No. Analysis runs locally. Your agent sees the results, and its provider has its own data policy.

Any agent that supports local MCP servers can use it.

Update first, because a recent release may already include the fix. If the problem continues, open an issue on GitHub with your REA version, the target type, the steps to reproduce, and the error output.

The old problem was simple: understanding software without source code took too much skill, too many tools, and too much time. REA’s answer is just as simple. It gives your AI agent the tools to investigate, and it requires the agent to show its evidence. Whether you want to learn how a favorite feature works, study a classic game, or inspect an Electron app, REA is a strong place to start. Just make sure you use it only on software you are allowed to examine.

REA: The Open-Source AI Tool That Can Reverse Engineer Almost Anything (2026 Guide)

#9528. Heavy cream vs. whipping cream: What's the difference?: Understanding the right cream for your baking.

If you’re baking a recipe that calls for heavy cream, or picking up a carton to turn into whipped cream to finish a dessert, you may be confused when you hit the dairy aisle. There’s “heavy cream” — but also “heavy whipping cream” or, in some cases, just “whipping cream.”

So when it comes to heavy cream versus whipping cream, is there truly a difference?

Aside from being delicious, there are very specific definitions and standards that must be met in order for something to be labeled as heavy cream. It is made by separating the fatty top layer from the base milk layer during processing. The FDA states that heavy cream is cream that contains no less than 36% milk fat.  Comparatively, milk has 0% to around 3% milk fat, as well as a higher water concentration. Because of its fat content, heavy cream retains a rich taste and, when whipped, it excels at creating stiff peaks that hold their shape for a long time.

Whipping cream — sometimes called “heavy whipping cream” — is made using a similar process as heavy cream and is also the milk fat removed before milk is homogenized. However, whipping cream can contain somewhere between 30% and 35% milk fat content, according to FDA regulations. Because of its slightly lower fat content, it whips into a softer, more billowy cream, and it will deflate more quickly than whipped cream made with heavy cream.

Luckily, the difference in taste and performance between the two types of cream are not very discernible. This means you can use them interchangeably in recipes — and it's okay if you accidentally buy the "wrong" one. Both can yield a delicious bowl of homemade whipped cream. (Can’t justify buying a whole carton of either one? We’ve got you covered with an easy homemade heavy cream substitute.)

A note on King Arthur recipes: The King Arthur Test Kitchen prefers heavy cream in most instances, particularly when making whipped cream, because of the higher fat content. That said, you can substitute heavy whipping cream 1:1 in any King Arthur recipe that calls specifically for heavy cream without any issue.

As a general rule of thumb, use heavy cream for making stable whipped cream for topping pies, layered desserts like tiramisu or banana pudding, and any sweet where the structural integrity hinges on the cream really holding its shape. Heavy cream can also be handy for making cream scones and drop biscuits, where the richness of the dairy can shine through. For more heavy cream baking inspiration, check out these 12 recipes that call on heavy cream.

#9522. How to clean cast iron  : It’s simpler than you think.

Despite what you may have heard, cleaning and maintaining a cast iron skillet or Dutch oven isn’t difficult. It’s practically impossible to ruin a well-seasoned skillet, and despite your best efforts, sometimes food will stick. If your cast iron is covered in stuck-on bits of cheese from a batch of Crispy Cheesy Pan Pizza, here's how to clean it.

We can settle the debate once and for all: Yes, you can use soap to clean your cast iron. Dishwashing soap will not damage the seasoning that makes your skillet non-stick. Polymerized oil creates the layer of seasoning through heat, and dish soap isn’t strong enough to break that bond.

No, you cannot clean a cast iron skillet in the dishwasher. This will degrade the seasoning layer and cause it to rust.

You should not soak a cast iron pan either; the water will cause it to rust. If you do end up rusting your pan, you can still rescue it by scrubbing off the rust then re-seasoning the pan.

Using warm, soapy water, scrub the pan with a stiff-bristled brush or sponge to remove any food residue. Avoid harsh, abrasive scrubbers like steel wool or metal pads, which can strip the pan of its seasoning.

Once cleaned, fully dry the pan with a kitchen towel, or place it onto a burner over low heat so the water fully evaporates. Don’t walk away from the pan — it can quickly get smoky once the water has evaporated.

Regardless of which method you prefer, it’s imperative that the pan is fully dry. Water (not soap!) is the enemy of cast iron, which can cause it to rust. Once dry, add a few drops of neutral oil and spread all over the pan with a towel.

Photography by Patrick Marinello; styling by Yekaterina Boytsova

#9517. How to proof bread in the oven: Common challenge, simple solution.

During proofing, bread and other yeasted doughs do best in a temperature-controlled, humid, draft-free environment. Your kitchen counter may not cut it (especially in colder months), but is there a corner of your kitchen that fits that description? Yes, your oven — and you don’t even need to fire it up!

Yeast dough is happiest when rising at temperatures between 75°F and 78°F. It will certainly rise in cooler or warmer temperatures. But for most doughs, that range is optimum for both yeast development and bread flavor.

Your oven’s interior will pretty much mirror room temperature. And depending on the time of year (or how much you use air conditioning), that temperature could be pretty cool—too cool for yeast’s comfort.

To get the oven up to that ideal proofing temperature, people often turn to a couple of different methods. I decided to try a bunch of them to see which is best — and helpfully, there was a clear winner.

It’s tempting to simply preheat the oven for a minute or so to warm its interior; but not only is this hit-and-miss (How long should I leave it on? Will the oven get too hot?), it’s ineffective; the heat quickly dissipates once you turn the oven off.

Enter your oven light. When turned on, your oven light’s slow, gentle heat will gradually warm the oven to the desired temperature. After trying a number of different methods for proofing bread in the oven, including several listed below, this was my clear favorite because it created the ideal temperature (not too hot, not too cold), maintained that temperature for several hours, and was essentially failproof (no overshooting the temp, for example!).

It can take your oven a while to reach the desired temperature, especially if your kitchen is cold to begin with. With so many variables — season, climate, kitchen, oven — you’ll want to do a simple experiment to determine your own best method for turning your oven into an effective, efficient proof box:

Take your oven’s temperature before turning on the light. Then turn on the light and measure the temperature again at 15-minute intervals, to see just how quickly the light warms things up. For reference, the light in my electric oven takes about an hour to raise the oven’s interior temperature by 10 degrees, and another hour to raise it an additional five degrees; your results will probably vary a bit.

Warm your oven to about 80°F before turning off the light. Over the next couple of hours, the temperature will gradually drift down by about 10 degrees, giving your rising dough plenty of time in and around that 75°F to 78°F sweet spot.

Once you know how to warm your oven using only its lightbulb, think about maintaining humidity: Dry dough can develop a tough skin, which inhibits rising.

If you’re proofing dough in a bowl (or later, a shaped loaf in a pan), cover it with a clear plastic shower cap or reusable plastic bowl cover. Whatever you use, make sure it's large enough to form a “poof” on top, so the cover doesn’t touch the rising dough.

For shaped rolls (or anything else in a large, flat pan), use an extra-large shower cap; or simply drape the pan with well-greased plastic wrap, waxed paper, or parchment.

What if your oven doesn’t have a light, the lightbulb only lights when you open the oven door, or it’s a “cool” LED bulb?

Then your best bet is a pan of boiling water set on the lowest rack, which will both warm and humidify your oven’s interior. Place the bread dough on the oven’s middle rack; no need to cover it.  Set a shallow pan (e.g., 9" x 13" pan) on the lower rack, and add four cups of boiling water. Quickly close the oven door.

Your oven’s temperature will immediately rise by about 30 degrees, which will probably be warmer than you want. Cool it down by opening the door wide for about five minutes; the temperature should drop about 15 degrees.

As the water in the oven cools, the air around it cools, too. But it happens so gradually that your oven should still remain sufficiently warm for the one to two hours your bread typically needs to rise. For longer-rising breads, simply switch out the cool water with another pan of hot water, if necessary.

Some ovens actually have a proof setting or proofing drawer. I don’t always love using this setting, though: Most are programmed to temperatures ranging from 90°F to 100°F, far warmer than yeast dough’s optimal 75°F to 78°F. For best results, figure out how long it takes to reach about 80°F, then turn it off.

Tip #1: If you have to open the oven door to check your rising dough, don’t worry. Unlike the huge 15- to 20-degree drop you experience when opening a fully heated oven, the temperature inside your light- or steam-warmed oven will only drop by a degree or two.

Tip #2: Typically, you don’t preheat your oven with rising dough inside. So when your dough is close to fully risen, remove it from the oven and set it somewhere safe. (If there’s room, the top of your fridge is both warm and out of harm’s way.) Timed just right, your bread will be perfectly proved by the time the oven finishes preheating.

Tip #3: To prevent someone from killing your rising dough by turning on the oven (say, to warm their leftover pizza), write “NO!” on a sticky note and affix it to the oven’s start button. Really!

For the highly passionate bread baker (or a small baking business), an electronic proof box like the Brod & Taylor Proofer Pro is a step up from proofing dough in the oven. It controls temperature with exquisite precision, from cold-proofing (down to 41°F) for those overnight ferments up to 122°F for an express warmup, all while ensuring perfect humidity. Wi-Fi and programmable timers let you control your dough’s development for up to eight days. It’s literally set it and forget it — the process is simple, but the results are simply amazing.

Still looking for a warm, draft-free spot for your rising bread dough? Think beyond your oven to other major appliances: Both your clothes dryer and dishwasher can double as a proof box!

Cover photo by Mark Weinberg; food styling by Liz Neily.

#9513. The secret to make-ahead pie crust? Pie crumbs.: Get ahead on your pie baking right now.

'Tis the season — to start thinking about holiday baking. And while this time of year is full of joy and celebration, it can also be stressful. We’re all searching for ways to get ahead of the curve, and one of the easiest? Make-ahead pie crust, made using pie crumbs.

I first learned of this technique from a 90-something friend with whom I love to talk baking. Over lunch one day, something she said about pie captured my attention.

"Did you ever hear of pie crumbs?" she asked. I admitted I hadn't — aside from the obvious: the scraps of pie crust left on the plate after the slice is gone. "My mother used to mix flour and salt and lard together to make this crumbly mixture that she'd store in a crock in the cellar. She called them her pie crumbs. When she wanted to make a pie, she'd just scoop out a few handfuls, add water, and roll out her crust."

Sounds like a good make-ahead solution for 100 years ago — but now that we have easy access to freezers, why not just make pie dough and freeze it in ready-to-roll disks? A couple of reasons, actually.

1) Pie crumbs allow you to make any amount of crust, from mini apple pies to a crust for a deep-dish 10" pie. With frozen disks, you're looking at a standard single crust — not always exactly what you want.

2) Pie crumbs save time. Remove however much of the crumbly mixture you need (more on this below) from the freezer, and within 15 minutes the fat is soft enough that you can add water and roll out your crust. Compare that to the hours it takes to thaw and roll a frozen disk of prepared crust — not to mention the elbow grease if your crust isn’t fully thawed.

3) Pie crumbs can be more stable in the freezer than pie crust disks. Why? Because without the added water, no ice crystals form. Ice crystals can damage the flour/water matrix, leading to changes in its structure (which can then potentially lead to changes in your pie crust).

Oh, and one other reason I like pie crumbs: If my friend's mother used them, they were probably a 19th-century kitchen time-saver. And I love the feeling of preserving and carrying forward our American baking traditions — even something as simple as a shortcut for pie crust.

Choose a standard pie crust recipe: Our Classic Double Pie Crust recipe is good choice, but anything that involves cutting fat into flour (lard, shortening, butter, etc.) will work.

Mix flour, salt, and shortening and/or butter: Follow your recipe up until all of the fat is incorporated into the flour. You should be left with a bowl of dry, crumbly dough that barely holds together when squeezed. If using butter, you should be able to see visible chunks scattered throughout the dough.

Weigh the pie crumbs: If you’re making a large batch of pie crumbs, it’s helpful to weigh and label the total gram amount so that you can easily remove the amount of pie crumbs for a single pie crust as needed. Our Classic Double Pie Crust makes 488 grams of pie crumbs; that means 244 grams per single pie crust. Label these amounts on your freezer storage bag.

Bag, label, and freeze the crumbs: Seal pie crumbs in an airtight, freezer-safe bag and place in the freezer, preferably in the back where it won't be subject to warm air wafting over it each time you open the freezer door.

Scoop crumbs out of the bag into a bowl: Whether one crust, two crusts, or one and a half, do the math and measure the crumbs based on your recorded gram amounts.

Let the crumbs thaw for 15 to 20 minutes or so: Wait until the butter chunks feel barely pliable in your fingers.

Add water and mix: Add water based on your original recipe amount, or just enough water to make a chunky mass when mixed. Squeeze and knead the dough briefly; all you're doing here is bringing the chunks together into one solid piece of dough.

Roll the dough, place in a pan, and bake accordingly: From here, your pie crust is the same as any fresh-made crust and can be filled and baked or prebaked for a no-bake filling. (Bonus: Because the crumbs were frozen and remain cold as you work with them, there's no need to chill your rolled-out crust before filling and/or baking.)

Fairly indefinitely, though the longer they're frozen, the more chance they have both to absorb freezer odors, and for the fats to start to go off. I've also found that, after about two weeks in the freezer, I need to add a touch more water than usual to bring the dough together — due to the drying effects inherent in freezing.

With pie season hard upon us, now's the time to try pie crumbs for make-ahead pie crust. Or maybe you have another old-fashioned pie trick up your sleeve? Share your favorite tips in the comments, below.

For detailed ingredient amounts for the crust demonstrated above, see our recipe for Classic Double Pie Crust.

And if you're looking for additional time-saving ways to use your freezer in the run-up to the holidays, check out our recipe for Homemade Brown and Serve Rolls and Apple Pie with Make-Ahead Filling.

#9510. Skip The Pan: Grilled Cheese Is 10x Crispier When You Cook It Like This

Whether you like it on its own or coupled with a bowl of roasted tomato soup, a grilled cheese is one of life's simple pleasures. Making one for yourself is simple enough in a pan or skillet. However, preparing half a dozen or more can be a pretty big undertaking on the stovetop. Fortunately, there's an easier way. By using a couple of baking sheets and your oven, you can conveniently whip up a large batch of these cheesy sandwiches that come out super crispy.

This technique mimics a panini press, which functions by heating top and bottom metal plates connected by a hinge. This gets both sides of the sandwich crispy at the same time, eliminating the need for flipping. However, these presses have their downsides. The weight of the plates, for instance, can turn softer bread into a pancake. Baking sheets, on the other hand, are much lighter and won't compromise the integrity of more delicate breads.

The oven also has the advantage of providing ambient heat since it's an enclosed environment. This means that your sandwich is getting heated on all sides instead of just the top and bottom, helping to create crisp crusts and melted cheese. However, you still need to preheat your top baking sheet for even crispness, since the bottom of your sandwiches could brown before the tops get crispy.

Depending on how many sandwiches you want to prepare, you can vary the size of the baking sheet you use. To make about six to eight at once, use a half-sheet pan, which measures about 18 inches by 13 inches and is probably the size you have at home. You can also use a quarter-sheet pan if you want to make fewer.

While the fat you spread on your bread (we recommend mayo for the crispiest results) will help ensure that your sandwiches don't stick to the baking sheets, you can also take a tip from Ina Garten and use parchment paper to line the pans for extra insurance. Also, don't stick to just using your baking sheets right side up. In fact, using your bottom pan upside down will allow for more airflow since the rim won't get in the way, thus crisping your sandwiches more effectively.

To make this technique really work, though, you're going to need to make sure you choose the right kind of cheese that will melt easily by the time the crusts of your sandwiches become golden brown. After all, you don't want to have to keep putting your grilled cheeses back in the oven to finish melting. The best options have a good balance of moisture and fat, and younger cheeses tend to be the go-to varieties that meet this standard. Some recommendations include Havarti, Gruyère, and cheddar. However, you can opt for some underrated (but tasty) cheeses to give your sandwiches extra character. You can also combine several types of cheese for a more varied flavor and texture.

#9507. The Best Italian Olive Oil You Can Buy At Costco (And Where It Comes From)

One of the best perks of a Costco membership is exclusive access to its wide range of bulk bargain buys. Its Italian section is among the most impressive, where you can purchase a 72-pound wheel of Parmigiano Reggiano or keep things simple with some dried pasta. But no matter what Italian delight you're cooking up, a good-quality olive oil is where the magic happens. To help curate the best meal possible, we ranked 11 of the best Italian foods you can buy at Costco, and its Kirkland Signature Toscano Extra Virgin Olive Oil landed itself a well-deserved spot.

The oil holds a Toscano Protected Geographical Indication (PGI) designation, which certifies that the extra virgin olive oil was produced in the region of Tuscany, Italy, according to specific standards. Like most Kirkland Signature grocery items, Costco contracts with outside producers rather than manufacturing the oil itself. Unfortunately, Costco keeps its suppliers under tight wraps, so it's difficult to pinpoint exactly where the oil comes from ... but there's nothing stopping us from guessing. Interestingly, oil from Tuscany's Montalbano subzone has been noted to have distinct notes of almond and artichoke, which also happens to be exactly how the taste of the oil is described on the back of the bottle.

While the exact origin of the oil remains a mystery, what we do know for sure is that Tuscan olive oil sits among the best in the world. The region is home to numerous native cultivars, with three main ones making up the bulk of production. Another thing that sets Tuscan olive oil apart is its scarcity. The region only produces a tiny amount of oil compared to major producers like Calabria and Puglia, so consider it a privilege if you're able to get your hands on a Tuscan bottle.

Just by reading the label, you can tell this is an olive oil worth picking up. Extra virgin means the oil was extracted mechanically, without chemical solvents or excessive heat. Olives are crushed into a paste, then processed to separate the oil from the water and solids, all at low temperatures (cold extraction, in other words). Keeping things cool matters because excessive heat can strip away the delicate flavors and aromas that give good olive oil those fruity and peppery notes. That's a sharp contrast to regular olive oil, which is typically a blend of refined oil and a small amount of virgin oil. The refining process uses heat and other treatments to clean up lower-quality oil, leaving something milder and a lot less interesting.

Extra virgin olive oil isn't just the more artisanal option; it's often the more nutritious one, too. Unlike refined olive oils, it retains higher levels of polyphenols and other antioxidants, which may help fight oxidative stress and reduce chronic inflammation. Add in its starring role in the Mediterranean diet, which is widely studied for its long-term health benefits, and it's easy to see why nutritionists love the stuff. It's worth noting, however, that extra virgin olive oil generally has a lower smoke point than refined olive oil, which makes it particularly well-suited to dressings and light sauteing, though it can also be used for many higher-heat cooking applications.

#9504. Ditch Expensive Lamb Chops: There's A Cheaper Cut With More Flavor

Rich, tender, and intensely flavorful, a well-prepared lamb chop is always guaranteed to be a crowd-pleaser. Compared to chicken, pork, and even most beef, lamb doesn't come cheap. And sitting at the top of the hierarchy are lamb chops. However, a delicious lamb meal doesn't always have to break the bank. One cut that's cheaper yet packs far more flavor is the seriously underrated lamb shoulder.

Much like most premium cuts of beef, lamb chops come from an extremely small, sought-after section of the animal. A single lamb yields only around eight to 10 desirable rib and loin chops, making them a limited commodity. Already, without texture and flavor considered, lamb chops already rein in a high price tag. Tenderness certainly plays a part in their appeal, too. Lamb is typically harvested before the animal reaches 12 months of age, meaning its muscle fibers are finer and more tender than those of mature sheep or cattle, and chops happen to be among the most tender cuts available. Pair that natural tenderness with their limited yield, and you've got a cut that commands a premium.

However, a higher price doesn't always equate to a more flavorful cut. Lamb shoulder proves this. Unlike the scarce rib and loin, the shoulder is a larger, less sought-after cut that comes from a harder-working muscle. Naturally, it contains more connective tissue and is less tender, which helps explain its lower price. Don't mistake that for inferior quality. The shoulder happens to be a richly marbled cut, giving it a fuller, more robust flavor than the relatively lean chops. So if you're after that rich, slightly gamey taste of lamb, shoulder can be every bit as rewarding as chops, if not more so.

Because lamb chops, whether they're taken from the loin or ribs, are so naturally tender, they're exceptionally well-suited to quick-cooking techniques like pan-searing or grilling. This makes them worth the price if you want a quick, low-effort weeknight meal. You don't even need to worry about a marinade, either. High-quality, tender cuts like loin or rib chops already have a potent natural flavor that doesn't need to be boosted by a marinade. Even so, if you want to literally spice things up, put together a classic Indian-style tandoori marinade using a blend of yogurt, ginger-garlic paste, and traditional spices like garam masala, cumin, turmeric, and Kashmiri chili powder for a seriously elevated spin.

If you'd rather keep things simple, borrow a tip from the Barefoot Contessa and ask your butcher to french the lamb. Frenched lamb chops are simply lamb rib chops where the meat, fat, and connective tissue have been completely scraped and trimmed away from the end of the rib bone. The contrast between the pearly white bone and the beautifully browned meat provides the elegant wow-factor fitting for the price of chops.

Cooking lamb shoulder is considerably less hands-on than chops, but you pay for convenience with time. Its connective tissue means it's simply not built for quick cooking methods. Instead, shoulder benefits from low-and-slow methods like slow-roasting or braising, which allows the tough collagen to break down into gelatin, thus creating melt-in-your-mouth meat. If you'd rather have quicker-cooking shoulder meat, lamb shoulder chops have you covered. Unlike whole shoulder, thinner shoulder chops can be pan-seared or grilled — though it's worth noting that braising remains a far better option when you're working with thicker ones since they still have more connective tissue than your standard rib or loin chops.

#9502. Does Fluoride In Drinking Water Affect Intelligence? What The Evidence Reveals

Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

Could childhood exposure to fluoridated water leave a lasting mark on cognition? Decades of data offer clues.

Fluoride in community drinking water is not linked to lower adolescent IQ or poorer thinking skills later in life, a long-running US study finds.

Researchers followed a generation of Wisconsin school-leavers, examining cognitive performance from adolescence into their eighties.

Those exposed to fluoridated water did not show a consistent disadvantage compared with people whose communities had no fluoridation.

The findings address concerns that adding fluoride to drinking water to prevent tooth decay could undermine intellectual development.

Professor John Robert Warren, the study’s first author, said:

“Utah, Florida and many municipalities have chosen to remove fluoride from drinking water based on flawed studies that considered the IQ effects of exposure to massive doses of fluoride.

Because levels of fluoride added to municipal drinking water in the U.S. are so much lower, almost all prior evidence from those international studies is not relevant to U.S. public policy debates.”

The research draws on the Wisconsin Longitudinal Study, which began with over 10,000 people who graduated from high school in 1957.

Researchers combined school IQ records with historical information about community water fluoridation and naturally occurring fluoride levels.

Following participants into old age allowed researchers to examine whether childhood exposure was associated with lasting differences in cognitive performance.

Comparing communities requires care because their residents can differ in ways that also relate to cognitive performance.

Once those background differences were taken into account, there was no consistent evidence that exposure was associated with either better or worse performance.

The same broad pattern appeared when researchers focused on people who had lived in the same county since early childhood, increasing confidence in their estimates of exposure.

Overall, the findings suggest that growing up with fluoridated community water is not associated with poorer cognitive performance in old age.

The study was published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (Warren et al., 2026).

#9500. Forget Butter And Oil: Cook Steak In This Rich Ingredient For A Better Crust & Beefier Flavor

When preparing steak, cooks often focus on selecting the best cut, then preparing it with a specific method to an ideal doneness. Less emphasis is placed on the fat employed for the task — although what you pour into the pan also impacts both the flavor and texture of your meal. So skip standard pantry staples like butter and oil, and try a version with beef tallow instead.

So — what is beef tallow? It's essentially rendered beef fat, an ingredient that lends numerous advantages to steak night. Foremost is the ultra-savory profile: Tallow is made by slowly cooking down beef trimmings, resulting in a rich, meaty taste. This staple works as a flavor enhancer in addition to a cooking medium, complementing the deep, savory character of steak. And if you buy a higher-quality grass-fed variety, you may impart even more complexity, introducing earthy and grassy notes to your dining experience.

In parallel, beef tallow helps create a mouthwatering crust. The ingredient boasts a higher smoke point than butter and some other fats. So whether you're searing on high heat or finishing the steak in the oven, the fat can withstand high temperatures, enabling browning and Maillard reactions that create a terrific crust. That adds up to an elevated steak experience, all from swapping out the fat that goes into the pan.

Preparing a steak with beef tallow doesn't require any special accommodations. The fat is solid at room temperature and can be shelf-stable when properly stored, making it an easy pantry addition. You'll only need about a tablespoon per portion: Simply spoon the tallow into the skillet, where it'll melt and cover the cooking surface. It's a cooking medium that's especially effective on cast iron — whether a griddle or a pan — as it can also be used to season the cookware. You can also use tallow when grilling by coating both the cut itself and the grill grates with a thin layer of beef fat.

Any steak cut can be prepared in tallow; just note that it lends a rich flavor. So if you're making a mild-tasting filet mignon, for example, the addition could be overpowering. It's better to pair tallow with robust cuts like a ribeye, porterhouse, or New York strip, thereby producing an especially beef-forward meal. Otherwise, there's no need to worry about the details. Simply add a spoonful to your pan and sear away; this staple makes for a dependably delicious steak experience.

#9499. Evaporated vs. condensed milk: What's the difference? : Navigating the canned dairy aisle.

Navigating the dairy section at the grocery store is one thing, but when it comes to the canned stuff, how much do you know about the difference between evaporated milk and condensed milk?

Before we discuss what sets evaporated milk apart from condensed milk, it’s important to discuss their similarities. Evaporated milk and condensed milk are both concentrated liquids made from fresh milk that gets heat-treated until about 60% of the water content is removed. The primary difference between the two is the amount of sugar they contain and their resulting texture.

Evaporated milk will typically only contain lactose, or the naturally occurring sugars found in milk and dairy products. Condensed milk, on the other hand, contains around 40 to 45% added sugar. That contrast means condensed milk is much thicker (almost syrupy) and has a more pronounced sweet flavor (it’s no wonder it’s often referred to as sweetened condensed milk!), and evaporated milk runs watery in texture and is lighter in taste.

Because of the extreme differences in the sugar content and consistency, evaporated milk and condensed milk cannot be used interchangeably. There will be a very noticeable difference if you use evaporated milk in a recipe that was written to use condensed milk, or vice versa.

Using evaporated in a recipe that calls for condensed milk will result in a dessert that is too bland and watery, while using condensed milk in a recipe that calls for evaporated milk can make a dish way too sweet and thick. If your recipe calls for a very small amount (1 to 2 tablespoons) of condensed milk, you could get away with combining a spoonful of evaporated milk mixed with some sugar. But if your recipe needs one whole can of evaporated or condensed milk, be sure to use the correct type.

If you want to learn more about – and celebrate – the differences between evaporated and condensed milk, make this Tres Leches Cake, which is a fantastic recipe that utilizes the two milks with heavy cream in a luscious cake soak for dessert. For a different dose of double the milk, you’ll want to try this creamy, custardy Vanilla Bean Flan.

Evaporated milk provides richness and creaminess to dishes that are both sweet and savory. It’s often used to enrich custard-based pie fillings, like Hong Kong Egg Tarts, Delicata Squash Pie, and Pumpkin Pie. To round out your fall table and use up that can of evaporated milk, try the dairy ingredient in dinner recipes like Pumpkin Soup and Creamy Tomato Soup, or macaroni and cheese.

If you have an unopened can of condensed milk, you can also make dulce de leche with it. One way to go about it is to let it simmer in a pan filled with water for a few hours: Learn how to make it here.

#9495. Does β‑Blocker Use Increase Depression Risk?

The association between β-blocker use and depression was investigated in a population-based observational study recently published in the journal Drug Safety.

While depression is often cited as an adverse effect of β-blocker use, there is limited evidence supporting this causal relationship. To better understand the association between beta blockers and the risk of new-onset depression, the study authors analyzed data from the UK population-based Clinical Practice Research Datalink (CPRD) GOLD database.

“We identifed patients aged 18-80 years with an incident depression diagnosis between 2000 and 2016, and matched controls, and estimated the risk (odds ratio [OR]) of depression in association with use of β-blockers,” the study authors explained.

Findings of the analysis revealed an increased risk of developing depression among short-term users of β-blockers compared with no use at all (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.91; 95% CI, 1.72-2.12).

Among short-term users, increased risk of depression was mainly restricted to patients with a neuropsychiatric disorder taking propranolol (aOR 6.33, 95% CI 5.16–7.76).  Patients on propranolol for a cardiovascular indication were found to be at slightly elevated risk of depression (aOR 1.44, 95% CI 1.14–1.82). Apart from propranolol, no other lipophilic β-blocker or hydrophilic β-blocker was found to increase the risk of depression.

Additionally, no association was observed between long-term use of β-blockers and the risk of depression (aOR, 0.85; 95% CI, 0.85-0.94).

“Our findings suggest that the reported association between use of β-blockers and depression may not be causal but rather a result of protopathic bias,” the study authors concluded.

Bornand D, Reinau D, Jick SS, Meier CR. β‑blockers and the risk of depression: A matched case–control study. Drug Safety. Published online January 19, 2022. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40264-021-01140-5.

Psychiatry Advisor, a trusted source of medical news and feature content for healthcare providers, offers clinicians insight into the latest research to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes.

#9494. 8 Trader Joe's Cheeses To Try And 4 To Skip

There's nothing like going to Trader Joe's before hosting a party and stocking up on cool and unusual cheeses. It's the perfect time to try something new or introduce your loved ones to one of your long-standing favorites. Trader Joe's has dozens of cheese at any given time and it can be a little intimidating to narrow down the options. To help out, I sampled some Trader Joe's cheeses to determine which you absolutely need to try, and which you're safe to skip.

None of the cheeses I tried were bad, some just weren't worth it for one reason or another, at a time when we're all watching our budgets extra closely. As touted in Trader Joe's incredibly easy return policy, every single product has been tried (and loved) by a company representative, so the chances of ending up with something that's objectively bad are pretty slim. Still, there were eight truly standout cheeses among my sampling, and four that you can take a pass on. Prices may vary based on your location.

Cranberry Chèvre Goat Cheese is not the only fruit studded fresh goat cheese at Trader Joe's, but it was the first one the store introduced, and it persists for good reason! Despite its simple composition (a log of fresh goat cheese rolled in sweetened dried cranberries), it is surprisingly complex. It's creamy, tart, and sweet all at once, and the chewy cranberry pieces keep it texturally interesting. It adds a freshness that can help cut through the other heavy, rich options on your cheeseboard, and it's also super versatile.

If cranberry sauce isn't your preferred vessel for the fruit at the holidays, use this cheese in place of Trader Joe's equally delicious blueberry vanilla goat cheese to make a two-ingredient appetizer with puff pastry sheets. Or, serve the Cranberry Chèvre Goat Cheese with dinner and let your guests slather it on their rolls, instead. Perhaps the most inspired option is using the seasonally perfect fresh goat cheese as a spread for your Thanksgiving leftovers sandwich to take it to a whole new level.

Trader Joe's Comté Cheese is the kind of cheese you could expect to find at specialty cheese shop, and probably for a lot more money. That is, in part, because all Comté cheese is subject to Appellation d'Origine Protégée (AOP), which are rules that dictate how and where it is made.

The AOP stamp on Trader Joe's Comté is how you know it's the real deal and follows those same regulations. It's made in just one Alpine region of France (in one of about 134 small villages) using raw milk from one of only two specific breeds of cow, and it is aged for at least four months. The result is a Comté that is firm but creamy, with a somewhat intense smell and a delicately funky flavor. It's definitely one to try, but serve it at room temperature as intended to experience the unique aroma and taste of this strictly-regulated cheese.

Whether or not you have specifically heard of Emmentaler (also called Emmental) cheese, chances are pretty good that you have eaten it. It is the quintessential Swiss cheese that most Americans think of when they hear the term, though there are actually several Swiss cheese varieties.

Trader Joe's Emmentaler has a mild, somewhat sweet and nutty flavor that would be delicious on a ham and Swiss sandwich with Dijon mustard. Emmentaler is even the ultimate fondue cheese. So why is it a skip this time? It does not offer much to set it apart from a Swiss cheese you could buy at any other grocery store. Instead, spend your hard earned money on one of the other kinds of cheese that you can only find exclusively at Trader Joe's. Because, trust us, there are a lot of unique kinds to try at TJ's you can't get anywhere else.

Despite the fact that this Trader Joe's cheese is literally called Unexpected Cheddar Cheese, I'd never tried it, thinking it was just like any other aged cheddar I could buy. I was very wrong (and have since learned my lesson on believing TJ's packaging). There's a reason this cheese came in at No. 2 on our Trader Joe's Product Hall of Fame ranking, and if you've never tried it, now's really the time.

This cheddar has a really nice nuttiness along with its sharp flavor. It is harder and a bit crumblier than many cheddar cheeses, and has those distinctive crunchy crystals typically found more often in varieties like aged Parmigiano-Reggiano. Those crystals are formed during the aging of certain kinds of cheeses, especially in Italy, and are part of what makes Trader Joe's Unexpected Cheddar so delectable. The crumbly texture might not make it the best cheese for slicing up for sandwiches, but you'll enjoy it a hundred different other ways before it even occurs to you to care about that.

Trader Joe's Cheddar Cheese with Caramelized Onions has been my go-to cheese purchase for over a decade, and, all these years later, it still stands up. It has a softer texture than the store's Unexpected Cheddar, so it slices and melts it a bit more easily, but the caramelized onion flavor is where this cheese really shines. There's nothing else like it.

It isn't just onions and cheese, either. The flavor is accomplished by blending a caramelized onion marmalade with an English cheddar cheese. The marmalade has a depth of flavor thanks to cider vinegar, red currant juice, lemon juice, olive oil, clove, cinnamon, and ginger. The warm sweetness of the caramelized onion marmalade is expertly balanced with the salty umami flavor of the cheddar itself, and the little bits of onion throughout make it visually and texturally interesting. This is the ideal cheese to bring to a book club meeting (trust me) and goes well with virtually everything.

The double bottles of bubbly being popped open on the front of this cheese's packaging had me hoping for something celebration worthy, but Trader Joe's English Cheddar Cheese with Champagne just isn't it. It's a perfectly fine cheddar cheese, if a bit on the extra salty side, but I had to really concentrate to pick up on any flavor notes that indicated the presence of Champagne.

According to the ingredients, this cheese includes actual Champagne, as well as Marc de Champagne brandy, which is made by distilling all the parts of the grapes that are leftover after being pressed for Champagne. Still, I had to really search for anything I might call Champagne flavor, which was a letdown. At the end of the day, it just wasn't as delicious as the Unexpected Cheddar or the variety with caramelized onions, despite being the most expensive of the bunch at $12.99 per pound.

I don't think I've ever had a bad Brie, but I can confidently say that I've never had a Brie more delicious than Trader Joe's Triple Cream Brie with Wild Mushrooms. Admittedly, I'm a big fan of mushrooms already, but I'm so used to having Brie with jammy fruits that it never occurred to me that the cheese would really shine when paired with the earthy flavors of wild mushrooms.

Served at room temperature with crackers or crusty bread, it spreads like a dream and needs absolutely nothing to improve it. That said, there's nothing like a baked Brie to make a gathering feel like a party and this wild mushroom variety is no exception. If you're short on time, use your microwave to make a "baked" Brie. You'll still get the delicious, gooey texture everyone loves in baked Brie.

Something I didn't learn until I was in my late 20s is that not everyone eats the rind on Brie, despite the fact that it's completely edible (and delicious). If you're not a fan of the earthy rind, you're probably not going to be a fan of the earthy mushrooms in this cheese, either, but I hope you'll give it a chance.

Trader Joe's Huntsman Cheese looks very different from other options in the cheese case, with its defined white and orange striped layers. Those different stripes are actually two iconic British cheeses: double Gloucester and Blue Stilton.

The two cheeses work together beautifully. The double Gloucester has a smooth flavor with a somewhat firm texture, while the Blue Stilton, which has a Protected Designation of Origin, is sharp and a bit more crumbly (though it's also creamy at room temperature). While the streaks in the Blue Stilton are indeed mold, it's totally scientifically safe to eat the mold in blue cheese.

What I love most about this cheese, other than its very unique appearance that makes it perfect for entertaining, is that its a great introduction to blue cheese for people who are leery of its strong flavor. By pairing the Blue Stilton with the double Gloucester, the flavors are well-balanced while still being complex and delicious. Lure your guests in with the striking appearance and amazing flavor of the Huntsman Cheese, then hit them with the Grand Blue (more on that beauty shortly).

I really wanted to love Trader Joe's Pink Peppercorn Fontina Cheese. It's very eye-catching with its vibrant pink coating and I'd incorrectly assumed that pink peppercorns meant it would be a spicy addition to my cheese selection. Avoid making the same mistake I did and take a minute to learn all about the different kinds of peppercorns, including the fact that pink peppercorns aren't true peppercorns and are more closely related to cashews than black peppercorns.

Still, the company's description of the cheese suggests a level of spice that just wasn't there. Instead, the cheese had an almost sweet vegetal flavor. A closer inspection of the ingredients revealed that the peppercorn seasoning blend also includes freeze dried strawberries, strawberry powder, and dehydrated red bell pepper, which made sense in hindsight. The flavors ended up tasting a bit muddled, though the cheese has some promise if it were paired with the right cracker, fruit, or other accompaniment. While it's certainly pretty, it's not worth the effort to make it truly exceptional.

One of the great things about being someone who is unabashedly a fan of blue cheese is that I never feel bad taking a decent sized serving from a cheese platter at an event. Pair it with a crunchy cracker and some red grapes, and I'm in heaven. But even I didn't know that blue cheese could be as good as Trader Joe's Grand Blue Cheese.

This blue cheese is unbelievably creamy. I would have been hard pressed to crumble it unless it was straight from a very cold refrigerator. At room temperature, it sliced almost like soft butter and spread easily on crackers and bread. This is the blue cheese to serve with a black and blue burger, with the cheese melted on top of the patty, or on a pizza with figs, prosciutto, and a balsamic reduction. It's so creamy that I'd love to try it mixed into mac and cheese, if I can manage to make it last long enough next time I buy it (but the need to eat it straight-up might win out).

Havarti is a creamy Danish cheese that holds up super well to both slicing and melting, which makes it a great addition to recipes and on your cheese board. It has a relatively mild, somewhat sweet flavor that lends well to the addition of herbs, peppers, and spices. Perhaps the most iconic variety is Havarti with dill, and Trader Joe's version is worth adding to your shopping list.

Fresh dill is used in a lot of Nordic and Scandinavian cooking, so it makes sense that it's a perfect companion to a Danish cheese like Havarti. Trader Joe's Havarti with dill is absolutely packed with the bright herb. If you're the type of person who loves anything dill pickle flavored, you're going to love this cheese. Add it to anything that could use an herbaceous boost, but I highly recommend pairing it with Trader Joe's Unexpected Cheddar for a grilled cheese sandwich that's out of this world. For a bright crunch that brings out the cheese's sweetness, add some crisp apple slices, too. Thank me later.

Prior to trying Trader Joe's Toscano Cheese Dusted With Cinnamon, I'd never actually heard of Toscano cheese. It turns out that that's because it's based on another cheese entirely, with a few important differences. Interestingly enough, while the retailer carries other cheeses with protected status, its Toscano is an interpretation rather than a faithful rendering of Italian Pecorino Toscano, which has a Protected Designation of Origin (PDO).

Italian Pecorino Toscano is a sheep's milk cheese made primarily in Tuscany, while Trader Joe's Toscano (both this cinnamon dusted version and other varieties it offers) are made from cow's milk in Wisconsin. There's nothing inherently wrong with either of those characteristics, and the cinnamon dusting on the cheese gives it a pleasantly warm sweetness, but it feels a bit like a bait and switch. The retailer describes the cheese as being like cheddar in texture and Parmesan in flavor, but I found that it was kind of bland compared to other options, and not even the dusting of cinnamon made it worth the buy.

To ensure a wide range of Trader Joe's cheese, I gathered varieties from all around the world and across many cheese-making styles. While I would happily sample every variety Trader Joe's has to offer, I stuck to a budget of $75, which still allowed me to splurge on a few options and sample a total of 12 cheeses.

Each cheese was tried  first on its own to allow its natural flavor profile a chance to shine. Initial impressions were gathered based on how much I enjoyed the cheese, how much of it I wanted to keep eating, and whether it felt worth it for the cost. That last criterion included considerations like whether the cheese was memorable and how excited I would be to introduce it to a friend. The following day, I prepared a cheese board with all of the cheese samples, two types of crackers, and warm toasted baguette, which I enjoyed with my husband while watching television to solidify my recommendations.

#9492. 19 non-traditional Thanksgiving desserts that aren't pie : Cakes, cookies, and even a tiramisu for your holiday dessert table.

Yes, Thanksgiving is a pie-centric holiday. But what if you don’t like pie? Or maybe you just don’t want it. Either way, we’ve got lots of non-pie Thanksgiving desserts, from spiced pumpkin cupcakes to sugary apple cobblers, plus plenty of autumnal cakes.

This adorable cake pulls double duty, serving as both a scene-stealing centerpiece and a feast-ending dessert. To make, stack two mini Bundt cakes together and frost with orange buttercream. Carving this frosted pumpkin at the end of the meal may just upstage the turkey!

Get the recipe: The Great Pumpkin Bundt Cake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Mini Bundt Pan Set

This dessert demonstrates how to dress up a crumb cake for fall: Top velvety sour cream cake with a juicy layer of apples, then crown the cake with a generous layer of apple pie-spiced streusel.

To make this recipe, you'll need: Instant Clearjel

Cranberry sauce can be a polarizing side dish, but everyone will love this New England-inspired cake, which pairs tart cranberries with walnuts and vanilla for a simple, satisfying dessert. (Because it’s so quick to make, this is a particularly good recipe for any last-minute holiday baking.)

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Sparkling Sugar

Sweet potatoes belong on the dessert table, and this recipe proves it. This ultra-soft cake is gently spiced and glows orange from the sweet potato purée, and it’s finished with a fluffy meringue that mimics marshmallow-topped sweet potato casseroles.

Get the recipe: Sweet Potato Sheet Cake with Marshmallow Frosting (make it gluten-free with Measure for Measure Flour)

To make this recipe, you’ll need: 9” x 13” pan

For a dessert that’s rich but not too sweet, turn to this recipe, which pairs pumpkin and pumpkin spice with chocolate chips. Baked in a decorative Bundt pan, it can be served unfrosted for an easy-yet-elegant dessert.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin-Chocolate Chip Cake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Soft Swirl Bundt Pan

Instead of apple pie, try an apple pan dowdy on your Thanksgiving dessert table. The pan dowdy is a traditional American dish from the 1800s and early 1900s. A combination of pie and pudding, the name comes from the method in which the recipe is completed: After an apple-based filling is baked in a crust-lined casserole, the baker takes a fork and "dowdies" the crust, breaking it into pieces that remain crisp despite being partially immersed in the juicy filling.

To make this recipe, you’ll need: 9" square pan

“Thanksgiving cheesecake” may not have quite the same ring as “Thanksgiving pie,” but when your guests are eating this ultra-creamy dessert, they won’t care. With its burnished top and custardy interior, this Pumpkin Basque Cheesecake reimagines the classic with bold autumnal flair, thanks to golden pumpkin purée and warm spices.

Get the recipe: Old-Fashioned Apple Cake with Brown Sugar Frosting

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Vermont Boiled Cider

If your biggest complaint about PSLs is that there's not enough coffee flavor, look to this Bundt cake, which has an espresso powder swirl running through the tender pumpkin crumb and a coffee glaze to finish the whole thing off.

Get the recipe: Pumpkin Espresso Bundt Cake

To make this recipe, you'll need: Golden Wheat Flour

If you don’t want to fuss with pie, we suggest making a cobbler instead. This fruit-filled version pairs juicy spiced apples with a crackly brown sugar crust — both prep and serving are easy, and the resulting cobbler will absolutely steal the show.

Get the recipe: Sugar-Crusted Apple Cobbler

To make this recipe, you’ll need: Vietnamese Cinnamon

Apples are great, but seasonal pears deserve some love too. This simple cake, made with a combination of almond and all-purpose flours, has a rich, buttery texture and an almost marzipan-like chew. Studded with fragrant cubes of ripe pear, it's an elegant after-dinner dessert.

Instead of slicing and serving dessert, bake every guest their own individual mini cake. Start with a moist, spicy sheet cake, then use a biscuit cutter or overturned glass to cut rounds for individual layer cakes sandwiched with cream cheese frosting.

Rich, silky, and balanced, this cheesecake is the kind of dessert that wins people (even cheesecake skeptics) over at first bite. The ultra-creamy filling gets its sweetness from brown sugar and maple syrup, while heavy cream gives it an especially luxurious texture.

Get the recipe: Caramel Macchiato Tiramisu

Make serving Thanksgiving dessert a breeze by baking up a big batch of cupcakes. These are packed with pumpkin flavor and spice, then finished with an easy swoop of cream cheese frosting. If you really want to level up your presentation, check out these cupcake decorating techniques for a pro-level finish.

Made by cooking cranberries with orange juice, then whisking the mixture with confectioners’ sugar, the icing adds a bright tartness that complements the rich cake.

Get the recipe: Cranberry-Orange Olive Oil Cake

To make this recipe, you’ll need: King Arthur Square Pan

#9490. Scrambled Eggs Are 10x Tastier When You Add One Store-Bought Ingredient

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

When you're a fan of eggs, they can be pretty delicious however it is that they come off the stove or out of the oven. Even so, sometimes you're in the mood for something that doesn't require a lot of preparation yet is adaptable and tastes delicious. That's where scrambled eggs come in. They have a beautiful texture — whether you like them super soft and slightly gooey or a bit on the crispy side. There are a lot of different techniques, and some ways to cook them are better than others – like cooking them in water is probably a bad idea. Following some expert tips for scrambled eggs can get you to full-on restaurant quality; for example, fresh eggs at room temperature will give you great-tasting results that cook evenly. But when you want to keep it super simple at home, you can improve your everyday scrambled eggs by adding in a little bouillon.

Either beef or chicken bouillon will work. Beef bouillon will give your eggs a deep, unctuous taste that can be delicious, but may be a bit heavy if you're not looking for something super bold. Using a little chicken bouillon, on the other hand, will add some bright, salty notes that still have plenty of extra umami. Chicken bouillon will bring out the natural savory, even slightly sweet flavor of the eggs without overpowering them — which makes sense because they're both, well, chicken. Whichever you choose to use, bouillon makes a super easy addition to your scrambled eggs that really only takes a few extra seconds of work.

As far as the bouillon goes, really anything will work — although it is often easier to get exact smaller measurements with powdered jars or pastes, like Better Than Bouillon Premium Roasted Chicken Base. Most standard bouillon cubes are equal to 1 teaspoon of bouillon powder or paste, but it can differ between brands, so take a look at the label. You'll want about a quarter teaspoon per three eggs. You can simply whisk the bouillon into the raw eggs with whatever seasonings and dairy you'd normally use (although you may want to lay off extra sodium because it's already quite salty), then scramble them to your preference. You can even wait to add the bouillon until the eggs have begun to set, then remove them from the heat and fold in the bouillon, so it just sort of melts in.

If you want to go beyond milk or cream, you can try it with a little crème fraîche, sour cream, or cream cheese, or even a Gruyère or sharp cheddar. Pepper is a must to bring out your egg's full potential, and you might want to even try a pinch of sugar for a hit of sweetness that blends in nicely — especially with chicken bouillon. As for the veggies and herbs, this trick will go great with pretty much everything you usually like to see in your eggs; just consider the flavor profile if you're using beef versus chicken. You can even use canned veggies in your scramble; for example, canned tomatoes are subtly sweet and tangy, pairing excellently with chicken bouillon while canned mushrooms add umami and even more depth to beef.

#9487. The Best American Burger Chain Isn't Shake Shack Or Five Guys

As one of America's favorite fast food items, burgers are something you've almost certainly ordered from a chain at least once in your life — but not all chains are created equal. Everyone has a favorite, so the question of which is best is bound to stir up some fiery debate. Even so, we didn't let that stop us from ranking nine of America's favorite burger chains, and coming out on top of our list was Culver's.

Founded in Sauk City, Wisconsin, Culver's now has more than 1,000 locations across more than two dozen U.S. states. Its flagship item, the ButterBurger, is served on a fluffy Kaiser bun, and customers have the option to customize it with a long list of toppings, including some world-class Wisconsin cheese slices. Living up to its founding state's nickname as America's Dairyland, Culver's treats dairy as a core part of the menu. Its famous Wisconsin Cheese Curds arrive breaded and gooey, while its fresh frozen custard is the perfect way to round off a meal.

Culver's uses fresh, never-frozen beef, with its cooked-to-order patties made from a flavorful blend of sirloin, chuck, and plate. But what really sets it apart from chains like Shake Shack and Five Guys is the seasoning. Culver's uses salt and pepper, while Five Guys forgoes seasoning altogether. The chain argues its beef is so good that seasoning is unnecessary, but not all customers buy that reasoning.

Meanwhile, Shake Shack does season its patties, but Culver's has one not-so-secret ingredient that tips the scales in its favor: butter. It's spread on the crown of the bun, which is then toasted until golden, adding a rich flavor that makes the bun just as tasty as the patty.

While the taste and quality of food certainly play a major role in where we rank a chain, they aren't the only factors to consider. On Reddit, one customer shared why they love Culver's: "[It's] probably the best [all-around] fast food there is," they claimed. "[High-quality] ingredients, consistent, always hot[,] and the restaurants are always clean." Which brings us to one seriously underappreciated category: cleanliness.

Just think about it: A good meal can quickly be soured by a grimy dining area. Fast food often gets a bad rap for the quality of its food, but when it comes to hygiene, the best chains can easily hold their own against high-end sit-down restaurants. Culver's is no exception, and customers and media outlets have even credited it with having some of the cleanest bathrooms in the fast food game, which can only be a good thing.

Beyond cleanliness, Culver's is also one of the few major fast food chains left that's still family-owned. Rather than answering to shareholders, the company still has co-founder Craig Culver as its chairman. This has seen Culver's put plenty back into its community, most notably through its Thank You Farmers Project; the chain's website states that it has helped raise more than $8 million for agricultural education since 2013. Much of that comes from Scoops of Thanks Day, when customers get a scoop of custard in exchange for a $1 donation to their local Future Farmers of America chapter.

#9485. This Thanksgiving, make your pies mini: Mini pies may be the secret to a stress-free celebration.

What’s the one food you most look forward to at Thanksgiving?

For some it’s the turkey. For others it’s the array of sides. But for many of us bakers, let’s admit it — our thoughts skip right over the apps and main meal and go straight to the pies, whether it's apple, pumpkin, pecan, or all of them together.

The problem is that for smaller gatherings, the need for multiple pies diminishes. Still, how can you bear to choose between apple, pumpkin, and pecan?

Enter the mini pie, a great way to showcase an array of pies and have them all disappear by the end of the day.

Here’s a potential hosting scenario this year: You’re serving six close family members (including yourself) at Thanksgiving dinner; you want to offer pumpkin, apple, and pecan pie. So you pull out your mini muffin pan and use it to make mini pies in a variety of different flavors. Everyone can enjoy one mini pie immediately, one later, and squirrel one away for the next day.

And mini pies aren't just handy for smaller gatherings — they can also make life a little easier during the frenetic rush of food prep in the days before Turkey Day. Helpfully, you can make these pies well ahead of Thanksgiving; they can be prepared, baked, and then frozen for up to a few weeks before serving.

Once cool, wrap each pie individually in plastic, then bag them all airtight and freeze. When you’re ready to serve, unwrap, thaw, and reheat briefly: 5 to 10 minutes in a 350°F oven or about 20 seconds (per pie) in a microwave will bring them back to life.

Because these mini pies have a higher crust-to-filling ratio, you don't need to prebake the crust to avoid a soggy bottom. Just place the pie dough rounds in your mini muffin pan, fill with about a tablespoon of the pumpkin custard, and bake.

Another benefit: The smaller amount of filling makes it easier to nail the bake. You don't have to look for a perfect amount of jiggle in your pie before removing from the oven — just bake until the exposed edges are golden brown and the custard is set in the center.

Turn to our Pecan Tassies recipe — a beloved Southern dessert, pecan tassies are basically just bite-size pecan pies. This recipe uses a tender, unsweetened cream cheese pastry, which cradles a gooey nut filling sweetened with brown sugar (no corn syrup).

We’ve saved perhaps the most beloved pie for last: apple. These mini apple pies are a bit more involved than the pumpkin or pecan pies. You need to precook the filling, and you have to choose how to top them. That said, they’re totally worth the effort (and the filling can be prepared up to five days in advance; store the cooled filling, covered, in the refrigerator until ready to bake).

Once you've precooked the diced apple filling on the stovetop to remove excess liquid, assemble your pies in your mini muffin pan by lining with rounds of pie dough and adding the apples. You can then choose how to top them:

You may be questioning whether making mini Thanksgiving pies is more trouble than it's worth. But helpfully, the techniques involved are very approachable — mix, roll, fill, bake — and the resulting pies are both delicious and just plain fun. Have you ever wanted a whole Thanksgiving pie just for yourself? You can have it — in miniature. Happy baking!

Do you say you won't dare bake pie because you're unsure of your skills with a rolling pin? Check out these other easy no-roll crusts: No-Roll Pie Crust and Graham Cracker Crust.

#9483. 8 Fish With More Protein Than Salmon

Unless you've been living under a rock, you'll know that protein-maxxing is all the rage right now. The conversation largely revolves around go-to options like chicken breast, but we'll let you in on a little-known secret: Several meats out there actually outrank poultry when it comes to the macronutrient. Among them are certain types of fish, a protein source that often gets sidelined in the conversation, but leaving it out would be a serious mistake. Aside from being delicious, versatile, and (much of the time) budget-friendly, fish is also seriously easy to cook.

Salmon may be the most popular high-protein fish, and 100 grams of the farmed Atlantic variety contains around 20.3 grams of protein. That's already impressive, since it beats the 18.2 grams found in the same amount of 90% lean ground beef and comes up just under 2 grams shy of chicken breast. Compared to other fish, however, salmon actually gets outdone.

Tuna sits at or near the very top of the seafood protein hierarchy thanks to its lean, muscular build, but beyond whole fish, another serious source of protein is the canned variety. At face value, a tiny, oily anchovy isn't much to look at. But once these fish are packed tightly into cans, you're left with a surprisingly concentrated source of protein, along with a healthy dose of other beneficial nutrients. If anchovies pack too much of a punch for your taste, canned sardines also make for an excellent high-protein swap — and that's only the beginning.

Salty, briny, and often budget-friendly, canned anchovies contain a whopping 25.4 grams per 100-gram serving. You can enjoy them straight from the can since they're already cured, or if you want to take a more elevated approach, take a cue from the Portuguese and use them as an elegant garnish on toast alongside capers, good-quality olive oil, pickled red onions, and a sprinkling of parsley for good measure.

Sardines might be tiny, but they're loaded with protein (around 24 grams per 100 grams, to be precise). Like anchovies, they're an oily, nutrient-rich fish, but they set themselves apart with a milder, less salty flavor. Often sold whole, they make for a visually appealing garnish if you're looking to add a little drama to your dishes, and since canned sardines have already been cooked, they're good to eat straight out of the tin.

Yellowfin tuna, also known as ahi, is one of the more premium tuna species out there. Alongside its firm, beef-like texture and clean flavor, it's loaded with protein, with a 100-gram serving containing around 24.7 grams. It's also exceptionally versatile, since suppliers cut it into loins, saku blocks, and steaks for a hearty meal, while thinly sliced or cubed pieces work wonders in a tropical poke bowl or as delicious nigiri if you're craving something lighter.

Bluefin is the undisputed king of tuna; it's prized for sushi and sashimi, and its price can reach heights that can only be described as absurd — a 612-pound bluefin once sold for $3 million at a 2019 Tokyo auction. Like its price, its protein content sits on the higher end of the spectrum, too, reaching roughly 23 grams per 100-gram serving. But bluefin is better known for its impressive fat content, with the fatty otoro belly especially prized for its smooth, buttery texture.

Tilapia is one of the most popular fish in America, and despite its bargain price tag, it delivers a serious amount of protein, with a 100-gram serving containing 26.2 grams. It's also a solid pick if you've got sustainability in mind, since responsibly farmed tilapia can be relatively easy on the environment. This lean whitefish has a firm, flaky texture and mild flavor that stands up beautifully to grilling or pan-searing, making for a quick and satisfying weeknight dinner.

Halibut is a fan favorite that just edges out salmon's protein content, with approximately 20.8 grams per 100 grams. Despite those similar protein profiles, halibut is a lower-fat alternative with a considerably less fishy taste, making it a popular pick for those who have yet to come around on salmon. There are plenty of ways to prepare it, and grilling, pan-frying, or baking will all make for a delicious meal.

Notable for its vibrant red skin, firm white flesh, and uniquely sweet, nutty flavor, red snapper is a hugely popular seafood choice that packs 20.51 grams of protein per 100-gram serving. Compared to your everyday whitefish, its price tag ranges from moderate to expensive, but it more than makes up for it with a wonderfully tender texture. To make use of its dramatic red hue, pair your snapper with seasonings and aromatics and bake it whole.

If you've grown tired of salmon's ever-rising price tag, look no further than rainbow trout. Also available as steelhead trout, this seriously underrated fish has a milder, more delicate flavor than salmon and leaner, finer-flaked flesh. Rainbow trout contains 20.5 grams of protein per 100-gram serving, though its leaner profile makes it less forgiving than salmon at very high heat, so it's best suited to gentler methods like pan-frying or whole roasting.

#9480. Forget Plain Bacon: Add This Crispy Ingredient To Grilled Cheese For Sweet & Smoky Flavor

Plain old bacon can elevate even the plainest grilled cheese, but it tends to be a bit one-note, contributing mainly salty, crispy protein. However, if you add candied bacon instead, that extra sweetness can transform a wide variety of cheeses and breads, especially if you take the time to prepare it with extra seasonings.

Candied bacon is a delicate recipe, but if you manage to make it without burning the sugars, you get an incomparably delicious ingredient for grilled cheese. The syrupy sweetness helps cut through the sodium, whether from aged parmesan or bread crusted with garlic salt, and the texture provides a nice contrast to gooey cheese. The smokiness, in particular, is a great flavoring agent that you can easily control by increasing or reducing the amount of bacon you layer on. The end result is a nice middle ground between turning grilled cheese into a dessert and keeping it exclusively savory.

Candied bacon can take a hot minute to prepare and cook, and while it only lasts about a week in the fridge, it stays good in the freezer for up to six months. Since all you have to do is let it thaw, then zap it in the air fryer for a few minutes at 380 degrees Fahrenheit, it's a superbly easy accoutrement to keep on hand for when you want something a little special.

The best part of using candied bacon is that while it may close a few flavor doors, it opens up so many more. You may not want to pair it with an herbed goat cheese or wine-veined cheddar, but it can substantially upgrade many of the tastiest underrated cheeses into something spectacular.

When considering what to add to your new sandwich, try to think about the types of cheeses you'd find in desserts. Something creamy and high in fat provides fantastic texture and an aromatic backdrop of flavor but still lets the candied bacon take center stage. Brie, Camembert, and mascarpone are all sublime with a bit of sugar, but when balanced with the savoriness of cured bacon, they become even better. Any pale, rich variety should do the job well.

You should always use a variety of cheeses in your grilled cheese, and a dash of something sharp and aged can balance out the powerful flavors of candied bacon. Microplaning some aged Manchego or provolone on top diversifies the flavors without overpowering them, and the extra-fine texture helps even harder cheeses melt more evenly. While you don't want these to be the main characters of your recipe, a bit of added nuttiness and earthiness can bring out the best in your bacon, even if you only add a tablespoon or two.
