#9477. 3 Dark Personality Traits Linked To Infidelity

Certain personality traits may help explain why some people betray a partner’s trust.

Certain personality traits may help explain why some people betray a partner’s trust.

Psychopathy, manipulativeness and narcissism are all associated with cheating.

The strongest average link is with psychopathy, closely followed by Machiavellianism.

Narcissism, which involves an inflated sense of self-importance and a need for admiration, has the weakest link.

Impulsivity, emotional coldness and a willingness to manipulate others may help explain why these characteristics are associated with betrayal.

The conclusions come from a review of 11 studies examining dark personality traits and infidelity.

Participants included university students, married couples and adults from the general population.

All three traits were positively associated with infidelity, although the strength of the association varied between studies.

Psychopathic traits include impulsivity, low empathy and a lack of guilt.

Someone with these characteristics may be more drawn to immediate sexual rewards and less concerned about hurting a partner.

A willingness to take risks could also make the possibility of being caught less of a deterrent — impulsivity and deception may help explain this link.

Psychopathy had the largest average correlation with cheating, although its association was close to that of Machiavellianism.

Machiavellianism involves a cynical view of others and a willingness to manipulate people for personal advantage.

In romantic relationships, these characteristics could make deception easier to justify when it serves someone’s interests.

However, a calculating approach may also encourage caution.

Someone concerned with protecting their reputation might weigh the potential rewards of an affair against the consequences of discovery.

This calculated approach could help explain Machiavellianism’s slightly weaker link with cheating.

Narcissism involves feelings of superiority, entitlement and a strong desire for admiration.

Attention from another potential partner may appeal to someone who places great importance on being desirable.

Nevertheless, narcissism had the smallest average association with infidelity and produced a less consistent pattern across the reviewed studies.

An inflated ego alone therefore offers relatively little information about whether someone has been unfaithful.

The broader picture may depend on how personality combines with relationship satisfaction, commitment and access to alternative partners.

Dark traits provide only part of the explanation for why people betray a partner’s trust.

The study was published in the journal Psihologija (Ataman & Yalçınkaya Alkar, 2025).

#9476. Skip Soy Sauce: Marinate Steak In This Umami Ingredient For A Delicious Flavor Boost

People love soy sauce for a next-level steak marinade not just because of its salt, but also its complexity. If, however, you want to eschew the sodium and bump up that deliciously fermented flavor, you need koji, a type of rice critical to Japanese sake production.

When you inoculate short-grain rice with Aspergillus oryzae mold, it slowly breaks down proteins and carbohydrates into an ingredient you can then ferment for sake or dry for use as a savory, shelf-stable ingredient. This is koji, a lesser-known source of umami that is nonetheless a potent marinade ingredient. While the differences are more subtle than with soy sauce, it gives you great control over your meat's final flavor profile and leaves you room to add other seasonings, like the best salts for seasoning steak, herbs, and spices.

If you use shio koji, a type of marinade made by combining koji rice with salt and water, you can even tenderize your meat. The sodium helps the beef retain moisture, while the enzymes break down proteins, leaving your steak tender and flavorful no matter how you prepare it. Just be careful, as some varieties have added sugars that can unexpectedly sweeten your meat too much. While they won't exactly candy your steak, they might overhaul your food's taste.

Whether you use wet shio koji or dry, shelf-stable koji, this ingredient is extremely useful and easy to add to marinades. Just keep in mind that its enzymes remain active when wet, so you'll want to be careful about how long you let your steak sit before cooking.

Dry, shelf-stable koji is quite versatile but may require extra steps. Grinding it into a powder and adding a few tablespoons to your marinade is a great way to boost umami. However, you can also create a dry crust on your steak and let it sit in your fridge for a couple of days. This can mimic some of the effects of long dry-aging, helping your beef develop an impressive level of complexity in only 48 hours. However, you'll want to rinse the rice off your meat and pat it dry before cooking, as its starches and natural sugars burn quite easily.

Shio koji is a bit easier to use and so delicious that you don't even need other marinade ingredients. Since it's able to thoroughly coat the meat, this is a great choice if you're working with tough cuts, like flank steak, that need some extra tenderizing. Two tablespoons per pound of protein should be plenty to get tender meat. To get a good crust, you'll still want to wipe off the excess rice and moisture and watch your heat, but it's an otherwise hands-off recipe that can taste like you spent hours fretting over the perfect marinade.

#9472. Not Cocoa Powder Or Coffee: Add This Pantry Staple To Canned Chili For A Major Flavor Boost

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

A good chili is a solid meal in a bowl that can be made easily at home in the slow cooker. It takes a lot of time, but it can create meals for days. There are plenty of different types of chili to enjoy if you want to try something new. But when you don't want to spend the time in the kitchen with all the beef browning and veggie prep, you can grab a pre-made chili right off the grocery store shelf. Some swear by coffee or cocoa powder to upgrade your chili, but there's one ingredient you likely have in the pantry or fridge that you probably have never considered. To improve the flavor of your canned chili, you should add a touch of jam or jelly as you heat it up.

Adding a fruit jelly or jam to your canned chili will help build complexity and draw out the flavor of common seasonings found in the dish — like cumin, paprika, cayenne, chili, and garlic and onion powders — while also offering a bit of contrast. It's like adding a pinch of brown sugar, with just a skosh of bright, fruit-forward undertones that can make it taste more like it's fresh, homemade, with subtle nuance usually lost in canned goods. It also helps cut the acidity of the tomato sauce that may sometimes be overpowering, especially in canned chili. Using a bit of the jarred stuff will even improve the look of your meal, adding a nice gloss or top sheen to give you an end result that looks like something right out of the page of a cookbook.

If you want to go with something gourmet that's relatively easy to find, a jar of Bonne Maman Strawberry Preserves, available online and at retailers like Walmart, will work nicely, but you can use homemade preserves or pretty much any store-bought jam or jelly, like Smucker's Concord Grape Jelly, also available online and in stores. In fact, jellies are often preferred because they blend in seamlessly, and you won't end up with over-sweet chunks of fruit in your chili. If you plan to use something with whole fruit, you may want to simmer it for longer on the stove, so the chili flavor will fully infuse with it. Grape is a pretty solid choice because it will beautifully complement the deep umami flavor of the beef without overpowering it. Fig and apricot jams also work great for some added depth and earthiness.

When it comes to your base, not all canned chilis are created equal, but this trick will definitely add flavor to whatever you choose to use. You'll want to start with about a half teaspoon of jam or jelly per can as you heat up the chili, then give it a taste once it's simmering. If it's not quite there, you can always add more, but hold back from going too hard right out of the gate.

Because of the extra sweetness, you may need an extra pinch of salt — although most canned chilis are already pretty sodium-rich. And some spicy additions, like fresh or canned jalapeños, red pepper flakes, or a dash of hot sauce, will balance things out nicely.

#9469. Add This Packet Of Seasoning To Pot Roast For A Delicious Southern-Style Sandwich

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Pot roast is one of those simple homemade meals that may take a long time to cook but is pretty hands-off in the Crock Pot. Just brown the meat, add your ingredients, and let the cooker do its job. There are plenty of ways to upgrade a basic pot roast and some interesting regional pot roast dishes, and this simple trick is a bit of both. To give your pot roast a hint of Southern twang, add a packet of dry ranch seasoning. Similar to a set-it-and-forget-it easy French dip sandwich but Southern, a bit of ranch in your pot roast will give you some delightfully intense flavor and get you darn near a classic Mississippi pot roast.

Ranch seasoning is basically an off-the-shelf, ready-to-go spice packet containing multiple seasonings — usually salt, onion powder, garlic powder, and other dried herbs and spices, like parsley and black pepper. Most brands also contain buttermilk and whey, which will add a bit of a creaminess factor, but you don't have to worry about the roast tasting like a bottle of ranch dressing because the mix will cook down with added beef stock and natural juices to form a nice, thick gravy. It will come out rich, bold, and savory with just a hint of tanginess from the buttermilk. Once your roast is nice and tender, you can simply slice it (or shred it) up and serve it Italian-beef or French-dip style, preferably with some melted cheese on top. The first bite through the bread into the perfectly tender and umami-rich, seasoned beef will make you a believer.

If you want to go for a more or less standard pot roast route, you can simply rub your roast with a packet of Hidden Valley Ranch Seasoning, available online and in stores, or something similar, and cook it how you normally would with beef stock, potatoes, onions, carrots, and whatever other veg you like to use. To go full-on Mississippi roast, you can forgo the veggies and slow cook it with the ranch coating, beef stock or au jus gravy mix, and a half dozen or more whole pepperoncini. Up the spice level with extra hot peppers or use the whole jar. You can even add a bit of the brine for some supplementary heat, plus a zingy kick of vinegar. This will get you closer to an actual Mississippi pot roast, which typically features said peppers.

For the bread, something that will hold up to the moisture of the roast is ideal. Toasted French bread adds a crunchy texture, but a toasted hoagie roll works great, and a thick sourdough will add a little extra tang. You'll want a cheese that melts easily, so you can quickly broil it without overcooking the bread. A simple mozzarella is an easy, mild choice, but a nice Gruyère will bring a richer and nuttier flavor with some subtle sweetness.

Ranch-seasoned pot roast or the full Mississippi mix is also great on egg noodles, mashed potatoes, or rice, or you can make a simple open-faced sando with a thick Texas toast. For an even saltier, more savory roast, you can try a three-packet blend with ranch, brown gravy, and Italian-style salad dressing mixes. However, to get that good Southern flavor, don't veer too far off the ranch.

#9465. The 9 Best Chain Restaurant BLTs, According To Customer Reviews

A good BLT is elegantly simple, a masterclass in culinary economy. With this sandwich, nothing is superfluous, nothing is forced. Instead, each ingredient works in unison to create an unmatched harmony of taste, temperature, and texture. Whether you're craving a light nosh or a substantial sit-down lunch, somehow a BLT always fits the bill. And because of its pared-down composition, every element has a chance to shine on its own. However, this also means there's no place to hide mistakes. If the tomato is a bit mealy, the bacon slightly chewy, or the bread a tad soft, it can throw off the entire sandwich.

These details make it hard for chain restaurants to nail a great BLT. They serve thousands of meals every day, and each individual order exposes them to a world of criticism and critique. To save yourself from a sub-par sandwich, you need to know which chains are executing a quality BLT. And this list hopes to do just that, featuring a handful of fast food chains and restaurants that are dishing up both familiar renditions and inventive interpretations of this classic sandwich. To find the best, I searched social media, roundups, and other online forums to uncover which chain restaurants are doing the BLT justice.

Cook Out has built a restaurant empire on selling comfort foods that you'd find at a backyard barbecue. From hush puppies to corn dogs to some of the best fast food milkshakes in the country. But it also offers a fun take on the classic BLT. While most people judge the sandwich's quality by the crispness of its lettuce, the juiciness of its tomato, or the number of grains in its whole wheat bread, Cook Out takes a different approach: speed, price, and efficiency.

These sandwiches are essentially BLT sliders: compact handhelds you can devour quickly and without a tummy ache. Despite their size, photos show you get a decent amount of each ingredient packed onto the tiny hamburger bun. And at a time when value is a particularly tasty quality, the fact that these mini sandwiches cost between $2 and $3.49 (depending on your location) makes them even more delicious. "They are ridiculously cheap," said one customer on Facebook. "Less than two bucks..." On Reddit, the feelings are mutual, with another commenter posting, "The BLTs are the unsung hero of Cook Out." Apparently, not all heroes wear capes; some wear bacon.

Sonic is another chain known for its nostalgic, carhop-inspired food. It has all the munchies you crave late at night: tater tots, root beer floats, breakfast burritos — really, the menu covers the gamut. But the restaurant is best known for its selection of classics, including the BLT. While some BLTs are light and dainty, Sonic's BLT Toaster is on the heftier side, perfect if you're craving something not greasy but still substantial enough to keep you full throughout the day. The sandwich isn't such a departure from classic BLTs, but everything just feels, well, bigger. The hand-sliced tomatoes, fresh lettuce, and trio of meaty bacon strips all come sandwiched between two thick slabs of buttery Texas toast.

Customers, say that they love the BLT, with one YouTuber noting it's "crispy, crunchy, and yummy." And speaking of breakfast, Sonic's BLT Toaster is frustratingly elusive. It's not discontinued, but it doesn't always appear when ordering online. A workaround is to get the Grilled Cheese and just add bacon, lettuce, and tomato. Or you can just ask for it specifically if ordering in person.

Potbelly knows how to put together a quality sandwich, and as far as chain sub shops go, it should be in the conversation with Jersey Mike's, Jimmy John's, and Firehouse Subs — at least that's what people are saying on the Reddit threads. However, like most fast food empires, quality varies by location. Still, a good Potbelly sandwich is as solid as any, typically well-stuffed, with a great ratio of condiments and toppings.

This same formula and attention to detail that make its Italian sub a customer favorite also show up in its BLTA (the "A" stands for avocado). Texturally, it's a terrific blend of creamy, cool, crispy, and crunchy, and unlike the more value-friendly fast food restaurants, the sandwich is assembled with a little more care. Customers note that the avocado is freshly sliced, the bread is crusty and substantial, and the pepper-crusted, applewood-smoked bacon is the best of any sandwich chain. "Potbelly makes an amazing BLT," claims one happy diner on Instagram. "...the lettuce and tomato are fresh and refreshing. The bacon is peppered, which adds a great flavor. The bread-to-ingredients ratio is amazing. Solid BLT 9/10."

Jason's Deli is more than just a deli. It has more than 200 locations, mostly in the South and Midwest, which is why it probably doesn't get the national acclaim it deserves. But Jason's makes some incredible food that's unlike anything else you'll find at other fast food restaurants and casual chains: giant baked potatoes, massive slow-cooked brisket sandwiches, and a bottomless salad bar that might just be the best in the country.

Its version of a BLT — aptly named the Bigger Better BLT — is no slouch, either, although it's sure to ruffle the feathers of BLT purists. Why? Well, the sandwich is stuffed with a few extra letters from the alphabet. Obviously, it includes the standard bacon, lettuce, and tomato — albeit in greater quantity than average —plus slices of avocado and a freshly cracked fried egg, all piled on two slices of multi-grain wheat. In general, customers are impressed by the amount of bacon and the overall sandwich composition. "This is my favorite menu item from here," said a Redditor after posting a glam shot of their sandwich.

From its famous #13 Original Italian to the Big Kahuna Cheesesteak, Jersey Mike's knows how to put together a sandwich. The chain takes the same thoughtful approach with its #1 BLT. Our sister site, Chowhound, ranked it the tastiest chain restaurant BLT around, citing the quantity of ingredients and textural harmony as key reasons for its success.

Jersey Mike's doesn't do anything special with its BLT. No bells and whistles or novel additions; it just nails the basics, with a precise ratio of tender tomato, refreshing shredded lettuce, crispy bacon, and a good mayonnaise (and some oil and vinegar or chopped pepper relish if you get it "Mike's Way"). The bread cradles the ingredients so nothing gets too soggy or, worse, falls apart.

On a Facebook post dedicated to the BLT debate, one person commented, "Jersey Mike's is the only place I will go for 'fast food' subs!" Others agree, with another poster noting, "...this was wayyyy good [...] I only wish I got extra bacon, but there was a good amount." And while everyone appreciates a simple sandwich, many customers say their customizations improve the taste, adding everything from tangy banana peppers to spicy chipotle mayo to your standard slice of American cheese.

Five Guys is known for its juicy burgers, thick milkshakes, and an unnecessary abundance of fries, but the fast food restaurant also makes one of the best BLTs of any national chain. However, Five Guys created some confusion among its fan base by formally "launching" the BLT sandwich just a few months ago, even though many loyal customers say it's more of a relaunch, given that it's been available for more than a decade.

Regardless, the sandwich is now available nationwide, which is good news for anyone who loves a BLT that doesn't skimp on the B. The sandwich is served on a sesame seed burger bun, but the applewood-smoked bacon is piled so high that it's about the thickness of a double (or triple) stacked cheeseburger. "They PILE the bacon on those BLTs," commented one Redditor, "...it's unlike any BLT I've ever had because of the sheer volume of meat." Facebook users have similar feelings. Overall, customers view it as an underappreciated alternative to the major sandwich chains, especially for the price, which is a few dollars less than Five Guys' standard burger. On a Facebook post comparing BLTs from other chains, one person commented: "Should have gone to Five Guys. That's the GOAT BLT."

Cheba Hut has been around since 1998, with its original location satisfying hungry students from the Arizona State University campus. Its menu reflects the playful, somewhat frenzied, college-kid mentality. Sandwiches are bold and inventive, with names and ingredient combinations that would make Panera Bread blush. Its version of the BLT — the Sensi Kush — has a traditional foundation of bacon, lettuce, and tomato, but it also includes a few, dare we say, dank touches that set it apart from your other basic sandwich chain, specifically a drizzle of sriracha honey, fresh avocado, and a buttery blanket of provolone.

Is this genius or BLT blasphemy? Based on customer reviews, it is most definitely the former. "I love a good BLT but I really love the Sensi Kush BLT from Cheba Hut! The honey sriracha sauce is 100," said one Facebook user, along with a pic of their sandwich. Customers on Instagram agree, with one commenter writing, "The sensi kush is fire," while another on Reddit said, "I love Cheba Hut! I think they make the best BLT I've ever had."

First Watch is a sizable chain with nearly 700 locations across mostly the eastern half of the United States. The restaurant offers a diverse lineup that emphasizes freshness and ingredient quality over speed and cost. At First Watch, there's something for everyone: lemon ricotta pancakes, power breakfast bowls, Benedicts, elaborate, lunch-y salads, etc., but when it comes to sandwiches, its BLT(E) is one of the best.

It pairs your typical BLT with two over-hard eggs (can't have messy yolks getting everything soggy) and Monterey Jack cheese — all on its artisan whole-grain bread. BLT snobs may scoff at the extra ingredients, but the bread, along with the sandwich's overall engineering, is as good as you'll find at a local cafe or diner. The portion is sizable, bordering on two portions-worth. The sandwich's flavor takes people by surprise as well, with it being filling and tasty while not weighing you down. One Instagram post noted, "I enjoyed the BLTE [...]. It was so good.  [...] I think I might start orderind sandwiches at First Watch each time I go." For something even more out there, try First Watch's BLT Benedict, which is basically an open-faced BLT sandwich topped with poached eggs and hollandaise.

Celebrity endorsements don't mean everything, but John Oliver (the star of HBO's Last Week Tonight) once publicly stated to his friend Stephen Colbert that his favorite sandwich is none other than a Wawa BLT. But this shouldn't be such a shock. Wawa is famous for its reasonably priced subs and sandwiches, and its BLT doesn't disappoint (at least when the bacon is properly cooked). While a Tasting Table ranking didn't put the BLT at the top of the list, the author still praised the sandwich, saying it was "perfectly built...nicely slathered with creamy mayo and stuffed with strips of bacon, shredded lettuce, and sliced tomato."

Some chains (even a few on this list) are guilty of — every so often — skimping on ingredients. Not Wawa. Its sandwiches are pretty stuffed. One Facebook user said, "The BLT hyperfixation is in fullllllll effect." Even if you do end up with a thin sandwich, the staff will gladly remake it to your liking. Another ordering tip: Wawa recently moved the BLT from the "cold" to "hot" sandwich section, which has caused some confusion amongst customers over fears that it had been discontinued.

To find the chain restaurants with the best BLTs that delivered on taste, price, and overall value, we dug through dozens of online forums, social media video reviews, and taste tests from within the past year. In the end, this list represents some of the best BLTs you can find, based on photos, reviews, and customer feedback.

#9458. Not Mayo Or Butter: Grilled Cheese Is Even Tastier With One Creamy Store-Bought Ingredient

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

A classic grilled cheese is a thing of both beauty and comfort. And of course, a simple sandwich such as this is open to interpretation, with many putting their own spin on it, like making it Swiss-style with raclette cheese or switching up the grilling process by using an air fryer, like Ree Drummond. But there's an easy addition you can make to your next grilled cheese that will make it even tastier (and it's not mayo or butter, though you can certainly use either): It's store-bought caramelized onion dip.

When spread onto the bread and covered in cheese, then warmed through in a hot pan, caramelized onion dip brings a burst of flavor and a compelling texture to the sandwich. Of course, it's definitely savory, but the caramelized onions also introduce a subtly sweet element to grilled cheese, creating a flavor sensation that is much more interesting for your taste buds. Meanwhile, the dip melts into the cheese, adding to the creaminess, while the onions introduce a little toothsome variety to chew on, beyond the softness of the filling and the crispness of the bread.

Trader Joe's Caramelized Onion Dip is one great store-bought option, and it's part of the store's regular lineup, so you should be able to find it year-round (unless it has sold out). Whole Foods also sells a version under its 365 brand, which Amazon Prime members can shop for on Amazon.

If you have the desire to take things a step further, you might try a mix-in or two that can elevate the taste of the dip (and therefore, your entire sandwich). That might include some dried cranberries, which can help draw out the aforementioned sweetness of the onions, creating an even bolder contrast in your salty grilled cheese. You also might play to the richness and crumble up some crisp bacon into the base. Or enhance the savory, aromatic vibes by adding both thinly sliced scallions and chives.

Now, if you're having trouble finding caramelized onion dip at your grocery store, you could always make your own, though cooking down the onions properly can be laborious. If standing over your stove for 45 minutes doesn't appeal to you, Ina Garten cuts down on the time by using a larger pot, which allows the onions to cook more evenly and efficiently. But if you'd rather skip the cooking altogether, you might find the adjacent caramelized onion jam on store shelves. This won't be as creamy as the dip, but it will still impart that same rich, savory, and slightly sweet flavor, so it's a decent substitution.

#9457. The best Thanksgiving baking tips from Ina Garten, Erin McDowell, and more pro bakers: Top tips from the Things Bakers Know podcast.

It’s the most wonderful baking season of the year, and to help you bake your best, we have top tips from some of the country’s best bakers, pulled from conversations on the Things Bakers Know podcast. Below, you’ll find Thanksgiving strategies from podcast guests Ina Garten, King Arthur’s Martin Philip, Erin McDowell, Helen Goh, and many more of our baking friends.

“The one thing I think people think they can do is multiply a recipe times four and think it’s going to come out fine, which it won’t,” Ina shared on her podcast episode. Instead of taking one recipe and just multiplying by three or four, she suggests either baking the original recipe multiple times, or doubling it and baking two or three times, depending on how many people you’re feeding. Just don’t multiply more than once! If you do, the leavening and flavoring starts to get thrown off.

If you’re baking for a lot of people, Ina also suggests making recipes scaled for a baking sheet. As she explains, “It’s easier to bake, and it’s easier to cut.” We’d recommend Slab Chocolate Pecan Pie, Pumpkin Cake Bars with Cream Cheese Frosting, or Walnut and Oat Slab Pie.

While you may be excited to try out a show-stopping recipe from a brand-new cookbook, Ina recommends resisting temptation. “You don’t want to test something you haven’t made a million times,” she cautions. “Even for me, it adds enormous stress.” Instead of turning to a first-time recipe, Ina highly recommends that you “do the things you know will come out perfectly every time.” And if you do want to make a new-to-you recipe this Thanksgiving, consider baking it once or twice in the weeks leading up to the holiday, so you have the chance to practice and work out any kinks (like figuring out make-ahead components or fridge storage) before hosting on the big day.

No one wants a soggy bottom on their pie, especially a super-juicy one like apple pie. Erin McDowell has lots of tips to avoid a soggy bottom, but her biggest one is to precook your apple filling before assembling your pie. “We can't necessarily predict how juicy any given fruit is, so even if you're using the same apple … each time, they are going to be a little bit different,” she explained on our podcast episode all about apples. Precooking the filling allows you to adjust based on the juiciness of the fruit you’re using that day. “If you're dealing with not-very-juicy apples, you may not have to cook it as long. If they're really juicy, you may have to cook it longer, but the process is the same.”

Pie crust can be incredibly intimidating for some bakers. But pie queen Stacey Mei Yan Fong says the key to success is sometimes to chill out, figuratively and literally. “The best thing you can do is just chill, as in calm down. You're not doing brain surgery,” she reminded Jessica in our Thanksgiving pie episode. “And also use your fridge!” As she points out, “the minute things start getting too wet or things start getting too warm, that's when people panic.” So take a moment to chill the dough and make it easier to work with. If the butter's getting soft or your pie dough is getting difficult to work with, just put it in the fridge to cool down for 10 to 15 minutes.

It’s not just the fridge, either — your freezer can also be incredibly helpful. Stacey likes to freeze her pies before baking, which she says helps the crimping hold its shape as it bakes. And remember that, as Stacey points out, “Pie is kind of a lesson in patience.”

On our special Holiday Q+A Extravaganza, King Arthur’s Director of Baking Education Amber Eisler has a crucial tip for avoiding runny apple pies — make sure you see your pie filling actively bubbling through the vents in your pie crust. As she explains, “It means the filling has boiled and bubbled, so the starches in the filling are actually thickening, which is a super important part of [avoiding a soupy pie].”

There’s a lot of cooking and baking happening around Thanksgiving, which means your oven can get pretty crowded, pretty quickly. But be wary of overfilling it. Even though your oven may have up to three racks inside, Martin Philip cautions against using them all at the same time. “Don’t make the mistake of crowding the oven when it comes to rolls. Let bread have its moment,” he says. Bake your pies the day before to save oven space; a turkey, too will stay hot out of the oven for hours. When baking rolls, you want “top and bottom heat, use your convection setting, make sure that air is moving,” says Martin. “Guard the rolls, y’all!”

Cookbook author and professional psychologist Helen Goh believes in the power of baking to bring meaning and fulfillment to our lives. During this busy holiday season, full of messy kitchens, family squabbles, lengthy to-do lists, and lots of hosting, it can be easy to get overwhelmed. But baking can actually be a calming, comforting activity right now. “Some people say baking makes them nervous because you have to focus,” says Helen. But part of the therapeutic effect of baking comes from forcing us to focus on a single task at hand. As she points out, “that takes you away from all that white noise about what you did yesterday or what's going to happen tomorrow,” and instead allows you to live mindfully in the moment.

Happy Thanksgiving from all of us here at King Arthur. If you run into baking troubles or just need a little support in the kitchen, our Baker’s Hotline is here to help.

#9454. Warning Letters Sent to Online Pharmacies Illegally Selling Schedule II Stimulants

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) have issued joint warning letters to 2 websites for illegally selling and distributing or dispensing schedule II stimulants, including amphetamine drug products marketed as Adderall.

The warning letters to kubapharm.com and premiumlightsupplier.com state that the websites are selling amphetamine drug products, including Adderall, that are misbranded and in violation of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Additionally, by failing to register the online pharmacies with the DEA, despite knowingly or intentionally advertising the sale of controlled substances, these websites are also in violation of the Ryan Haight Online Pharmacy Act.

“These letters are not only a warning to the companies that illegally sell prescription medications, but they also serve as a warning to consumers who have bought or have considered buying medications online without a legitimate prescription,” said DEA Administrator Anne Milgram. “Consumers cannot trust the safety or legitimacy of pills sold on unaccredited sites.”

In a press release, the Agency reinforced its commitment to stopping online operators illegally selling potentially harmful drug products to consumers. “These particular types of online pharmacies also undermine our efforts to help consumers safely purchase legitimate prescription medicines over the internet,” said FDA Commissioner Robert M. Califf, MD. “FDA will continue partnering with DEA in an effort to safeguard public health and protect consumers who need access to these important medicines.”

#9450. Add This Creamy Ingredient To Ground Beef For A Juicier Burger With Extra Protein

Incorporating secret ingredients into your burger patties elevates the dish in unexpected ways. Some components flavor the meat while others enhance the texture. For an add-in that does both — with a delicious underlying creaminess — look no further than yogurt. The dairy works as a ground beef tenderizer, making a burger that's softer and full of moisture. Not to mention, yogurt is an effective enhancement in chicken or turkey patties, too.

Yogurt's contained lactic acid functions as a mild, but nevertheless efficient, tenderizer, lightly marinating the meat. The inclusion of a liquid naturally adds lots of moisture to a burger — you certainly won't have to worry about a disappointingly dry result. Plus, the ingredient lends the burger a lightly creamy mouthfeel.

And if you use Greek yogurt for the task, you'll get a nice dose of added protein, too. Mix in a quarter cup of whole milk Greek yogurt — a quantity suitable for a pound of meat — and you'll up the dish by 5.5 grams of protein. This yogurt's extra fat content will further prevent dryness, all while forming a patty that's not too loose, making a burger rendition that stands out.

Working yogurt into your beef patties doesn't require any special technique. You can simply stir the dairy with the beef in a bowl, seasoning with salt and pepper in parallel. Follow by forming the patties as usual, then lightly brush the exterior with oil to prevent unwanted adhesion. Prepare the yogurt burgers using your preferred method, whether you're fond of using a skillet or grilling burgers like a pro. However, if you notice your mixture appears too wet, consider adding a binder — chia seeds are a fantastic option to absorb moisture but keep things tender and juicy; panko breadcrumbs will also absorb excess liquid while keeping the bite of each burger soft.

Such a burger tastes delicious with classic seasonings, but don't rule out creative modifications, too. The pairing of yogurt and beef recalls Greek and Middle Eastern cuisine, so consider integrating Eastern Mediterranean seasonings into the build.

A Greek burger spin could fold in oregano, lemon, and feta — core flavors of a Greek salad. A kofta-style patty might up the spice, working in earthy cumin, a dash of spicy harissa, and grated garlic into the mix. Alternatively, season the meat in a sweet direction by using simply turmeric and onions; the ingredients will set you up for a wide array of flavorful condiments. Build out the meal with an aromatic herbal yogurt sauce, a bold dose of roasted peppers, or a marinated arugula salad, and you'll make a burger rendition that'll become a frequent part of the rotation.

#9449. How to turn any bread dough into rolls: Transform your favorite bread loaf into shareable rolls.

So you have a beloved bread recipe that you'd like to turn into fluffy, single-serving rolls, but you don’t know where to start. We’re here to help — let’s get rolling!

Rolls are basically just tiny bread. Which means that, yes, you can technically make a pan of rolls out of any bread dough.

But first, consider the recipe and what type of rolls you're looking to make. If you want soft, fluffy pull-apart rolls (typically baked nestled together in a pan), consider starting with an enriched dough like brioche, milk bread, or challah. If you want crusty, European-style rolls (often baked on sheet trays), start with a leaner dough, such as this pain au levain.

Essentially, the type of bread you start with will determine the type of rolls you make, so plan accordingly.

Turning a bread recipe into rolls is simple: After the dough has had its first rise (otherwise known as its bulk ferment), divide it into small pieces, shape them into rolls, give them a final rise, and bake. The good news is that you don’t need to make any changes to the recipe itself — simply prepare the dough as written and leave it to undergo its first rise.

Once the bread dough has risen, it's time to divide it. Consider: How many rolls do you want, and how large do you want them to be?

Your best bet for even-sized rolls is to grab a calculator and kitchen scale. While you could divide your dough by eye, it’s faster, easier, and more accurate to use the weight measurements, if possible.

For size reference, the pre-bake weight of dinner rolls typically falls between 60g to 80g each. Imagine a 60g roll as the size of a plum when baked, while a baked 80g roll is closer to a Granny Smith apple. Moving up in the ranks are burger buns, which weigh around 100g or so pre-bake.

Here's how much each rolls should weigh before baking:

If you want small-to-medium dinner rolls: 60g to 70g

If you want medium-to-large dinner rolls: 80g to 90g

If you want extra-large dinner rolls or burger buns: 100g to 110g

Let’s say you’re using our Back-of-the-Bag Oatmeal Bread recipe. The total weight of the dough is about 830g. If your first thought is, “I want eight rolls!” you’re going to wind up with eight oat-y burger bun-sized rolls, because 830g divided by eight is just over 100g per roll. That's likely too large if you're looking to make standard dinner rolls.

To ensure you get properly sized rolls, it’s easiest to start by dividing the total weight of the dough by the weight of the size you want your rolls to be, rather than the number of rolls you want. In this case, 830g ÷ 75g = 11 large dinner rolls.

Once divided, it's time to shape the pieces of bread dough. If you’ve never shaped dinner rolls, have no fear! We have you covered, no matter the shape you choose. Basic round rolls? Got it. Fancy shapes? Yep. Braided rolls? You bet. And so much more. Often it helps to see the process in action, especially when it comes to hand positioning when shaping rolls.

For gluten-free breads, scoop the “dough” into a greased muffin pan rather than attempt to shape rolls by hand, since the dough is more like batter. If you're making medium or large gluten-free rolls, check out our Gluten-Free Dinner Rolls recipe for more details.

Small rolls won’t take as long to bake as a loaf would. Most will take around 20 to 30 minutes to bake, depending on their size. You can usually stick with the temperature your original recipe calls for, but 350°F is a safe bet, too.

A final note: Rolls baked close together in "pull-apart" style will usually take a bit longer to bake than they would if they were spaced out on a baking sheet.

And remember, if you make more rolls than you can eat in one sitting, you can always freeze and bake them.

We're diving deep on rolls ahead of Thanksgiving in our latest podcast episode, all about rolls.

#9448. Give Canned Baked Beans A Delicious Upgrade With A Drizzle Of This Ingredient (Hint: It's Not Honey)

When you need a side to go along with your main dinner entree and you need one fast, it's reassuring to know that shelf-stable, pantry-sitting canned goods have got your back. Included in Food Republic's list of inexpensive canned foods you'll use all the time are beans, and along with the plain black or red varieties (which typically need to be combined with other ingredients to make a reasonable side), you could also reach for scrumptious, creamy baked beans. But while they're totally fine heated up straight from the can, they can certainly benefit from a drizzle of molasses.

Molasses might not be the first thing you think of when you consider add-ins, but many homemade recipes call for it, and for good reason. Made by boiling down sugarcane juice or refining sugar, the rich, thick syrup is slightly smoky and sweet, with robust, burnt caramel notes, making it a perfect match for deepening the flavor of sometimes weak-tasting canned baked beans and bringing them closer to homemade.

It is for this reason that molasses is also preferable to honey here. Honey is intensely sweet, can taste almost floral at times, and has a delicate flavor, whereas molasses is bolder and has a meatier taste that can make its presence known among the other ingredients in the dish.

It's important to note that there are three main types of molasses: light, dark, and blackstrap, and they each have different flavor profiles. For canned baked beans, you'll likely want to stick with light or dark because blackstrap is intensely bitter (also, light is the sweetest of the three, so if sweetness is important to you, go with that one). If you're heating the beans on the stove, you can start by drizzling in about half a tablespoon of molasses per 28-ounce can, bringing the mixture to a boil, and then simmering for about 10 minutes. If you're baking them, likewise, just stir in the molasses before putting the dish in the oven — it couldn't be simpler.

If you don't have any molasses sitting about, don't panic. There are plenty of other additions that can help upgrade canned baked beans and make them taste less, well, pantry-fied. Take brown sugar, for example — did you know that it's often just white sugar and molasses combined? A little bit will still bring that sweet contrast to balance out the savory flavors and give you a deeper, more complex finish.

Another great option is one you might normally use on your pancakes: maple syrup. You don't want to use the fake stuff that's primarily made of corn syrup and artificial flavors and colors, but rather 100% real Grade A maple syrup for the best flavor. Its sweetness again deliciously contrasts with and enhances the canned baked beans' savoriness, while the maple flavor adds its unique caramelly, toffee-like notes to the dish.

#9447. Make Your Next Breakfast Sandwich Korean-Style For A Major Fiber & Flavor Boost

We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.

Think of Korean cuisine, and a sandwich likely isn't the first thing that comes to mind. However, bread-based dishes are widely enjoyed in the East Asian country, both in cafes and as street food. An especially popular breakfast rendition is gilgeori toast, a comforting breakfast sandwich stuffed with eggs and shredded vegetables.

Easy-to-make, packed with fiber, and delicious, the dish is a great candidate for your breakfast rotation. Traditionally, this sandwich calls for a fluffy loaf of milk or brioche bread, the buttery soft texture turning crisp on the outside once toasted. Meanwhile, the filling comprises a variable shredded vegetable medley: Cabbage traditionally forms the centerpiece, joined by carrots, onions, scallions, and often garlic chives. Mixed with egg and then pan-fried into an aesthetic golden-brown patty, the filling delectably complements the soft bread. Gilgeori is usually rounded out with a sprinkle of sugar and a drizzle of ketchup and mustard.

It's an assembly that easily comes together during bleary morning hours, yet nevertheless offers a nutritious start to the day. One sandwich can pack in around six ounces of shredded cabbage, which amounts to over 4 grams of fiber. Add up the fiber from a tablespoon of carrot, two of sliced onion, and two whole green onions, and you're including another 1.5 grams. Then, add in two slices of thick-cut brioche sandwich bread, and you've got an extra 2. That's about 7.5 grams, which is around a quarter of what you need a day, already knocked out by breakfast. Mixed with the roughly 6.5 grams of protein from the egg alongside filling bread, the sandwich serves as a terrific way to start the day.

The morning isn't always the best time to precisely reconstruct a recipe. Thankfully, gilgeori toast welcomes a wide array of reinterpretations and ingredients. Starting with the bread, feel free to swap the milk bread for sourdough, whole wheat, or even a convenient store-bought whole grain like Ezekiel or Dave's Killer. You'll lose out on some of the dish's airiness, but potentially gain extra fiber content in the process. Two slices of Dave's Killer 21 Whole Grains and Seeds contain some 8 grams of fiber, more than doubling the total of the sandwich.

Up the satiation further by adding on a slice of seared ham, a filling also enjoyed in Korea. And cheese is always welcome, whether American, cheddar, or fontina – Martha Stewart's go-to for breakfast sandwiches. Instead of the sugar sprinkle, lend the dish a sweet note by using jam: Raspberry or cherry jam makes a great fit. Not to mention, you can replace the ketchup and mustard with a condiment of your preference; you can buy a bottle of Gochujang Sriracha Hot Sauce online, for instance. The template of bread and shredded vegetables works with many flavors, perfect for morning enjoyment.

#9446. The two-second step to caramelize your pie crust : Just add sugar.

Most pie recipes will instruct you to sprinkle sparkling sugar or turbinado sugar on top of your egg-washed pie crust just before baking, so the coarse sugar can make those edges extra-crunchy and add a bit of glittery sheen. But why stop there — what if the bottom crust got the same treatment too?

That's what our Test Kitchen wondered while developing a new galette recipe for our newest cookbook (coming out next year!). While working on an apricot galette recipe, they tried adding a finishing sugar to the bottom of the dough before baking, and found that it created a crunchy, sugary, caramelized crust that elevated the entire dessert.

As an added bonus, this technique can help ensure a crunchy, well-browned bottom crust;  consider this step another line of defense against a soggy bottom, like baking your pie on a pizza stone or steel or baking pie on the bottom rack of the oven,

You can apply it to any pie (or galette!) recipe while rolling out the dough. Here’s how to do it:

On a lightly floured surface, roll the dough to a 10" to 12" round (aim for the smaller diameter for pie crusts, and larger for galettes). Sprinkle around 1 tablespoon of sparkling sugar or turbinado sugar all over the dough. (It’s important to only use these larger, coarse-grained sugars — we don’t recommend using granulated sugar.) Sprinkle lightly with flour, then continue to roll the dough to reach a 12" to 14" round. Carefully invert the dough round so that the sugared side is on the bottom of the pie pan (to make a single or double crust pie) or parchment paper (to make a galette).

Use this step in classic applications like apple pie where sparkling sugar can cover the entire thing, from top to bottom crust. Or, use it in custard pies like pecan or pumpkin. If you’re going the galette route for Thanksgiving, use it in our Apple Butter Apple Galette or Tiny Apple Tarts for Two. Regardless of the pie you choose, the crust — not the filling! — may be what steals the show.

#9445. The Vitamin Deficiency Linked To Chronic Headaches

Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.

Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.

Frequent headaches are linked to lower vitamin D levels.

People with chronic migraine have lower levels than those with occasional migraines or no headache disorder.

Lower vitamin D is also associated with greater muscle tenderness.

The vitamin helps muscles and nerves function, making it relevant to understanding pain.

One possibility is that low levels amplify sensitivity to pain, although this remains an explanation to investigate.

The research compared around 150 adults, divided equally between chronic migraine, episodic migraine and a group without headache disorders.

Blood tests showed low vitamin D in 78 percent of the chronic migraine group, compared with 60 percent of those with episodic migraine and 46 percent of the comparison group.

Average levels were lowest in chronic migraine and highest among those without headaches.

Chronic migraine means headaches on at least 15 days a month for more than three months, with migraine features on at least eight days.

These headaches can change in character, even within the same day, and can include pain resembling tension headaches.

Lower vitamin D levels were associated with more tenderness when muscles were pressed.

The researchers suggest that muscular discomfort and changes in pain processing could interact, potentially helping sustain headaches.

However, the association could also run in the opposite direction: people with migraine may spend less time outdoors because of light sensitivity or fatigue.

The findings do not establish that supplements prevent migraines.

Vitamin D’s established functions extend beyond maintaining strong bones.

It helps the body absorb calcium, supports muscle movement and allows nerves to carry messages between the brain and the body.

Deficiency can cause a condition called osteomalacia in adults, involving bone pain and muscle weakness.

The body produces vitamin D when sunlight reaches the skin, while food provides another source.

Oily fish, including salmon and mackerel, are among the best natural sources, while egg yolks contain smaller amounts.

Some breakfast cereals and other foods are fortified with the vitamin.

People who rarely expose their skin to sunlight can have more difficulty obtaining enough.

A blood test measures vitamin D status, helping distinguish a nutritional shortage from symptoms with other possible explanations.

The study was published in the journal Cephalalgia Reports (Prakash et al., 2026).

#9444. Not Cinnamon: Add A Pinch Of This Warm Spice To French Toast For A Flavor Boost

Warm spices on French toast create a cozy, aromatic breakfast dish that warms your sinuses as much as your tongue. While traditional cinnamon is always a solid choice, cardamom French toast adds new layers of fresh, almost herbal notes for something far more complex and just as compatible with your other favorite seasonings.

Some folks call cardamom the queen of spices — and for good reason. As flavorful as it is versatile, it's a shelf-stable ingredient that lasts a long time, grinds easily into a powder, and seems to taste amazing with just about any sweet recipe you could think of. While it can be a tad on the expensive side, small amounts suffuse your French toast with deep flavor, so even a small jar of seeds can last you quite a while. The key is to mix it with your other dried spices to create a delicate flavor profile similar to mulled drinks, festive winter desserts, and spiced ciders.

Six pods should yield about half a teaspoon of ground spice, enough for roughly six pieces of French toast (though pod sizes vary). Since you want a smooth batter without much texture, it's best to grind the seeds into a fine powder before mixing. The moisture from eggs and milk should help protect the delicate spice, but remember that heat affects the flavor release of spices. Gently toasting the pods beforehand is a great way to bump up the flavor without using more of the pricey ingredient.

Though cardamom has quite a bit of flavor, it's also rather delicate and can slip into the background or be the star of the show, depending on your preferences. In sweet dishes, there are few warm spices it pairs poorly with, and more obscure ingredients can really elevate its flavor for something showstopping.

Just about any warming spice you'd associate with the colder months should pair beautifully with cardamom. Cinnamon is a bold counterpart that can carry most of the flavor profile without overshadowing it when used in moderation. Allspice and cloves are a match made in heaven, providing an almost berry-like warmth to counteract cardamom's cool, herbal notes. Ground or fresh ginger can add a touch of sharpness that offers quite a bit of contrast, providing a similar bite on the tongue to garlic that's far more compatible with sugary bases.

If you really want to bump up the flavor of cardamom, don't stick to just spices. Floral notes from things like dried and ground orange peels, lychee, or guava really round out your French toast without overpowering your spices. These are highly compatible with cardamom and make your breakfast taste almost like a pomander, with an incredible bouquet of aromas the second your bread hits the pan. You can also use food-safe flavoring oils instead, mixing them into your wet ingredients for greater control over how much flavor you're adding.

#9442. Rising Fentanyl Use Challenges Current Methadone Induction Protocols

An increasing number of PAs and nurse practitioners (NPs) are working in addiction medicine including opioid treatment programs (OTPs) where they are increasingly able to practice autonomously. A recently released commentary in the Journal of Substance Abuse Treatment highlights the challenges that practitioners at OTPs face in reaching therapeutic doses of methadone for patients who are using fentanyl instead of heroin.1 The commentary authors noted that with “fentanyl’s increased potency when compared to other opioids, many papers have described the need for higher doses of methadone to achieve the therapeutic goal of reducing and suppressing opioid withdrawal and subsequent illicit ongoing fentanyl use.”

The commentary authors make several key observations and related recommendations. One key finding is that patients using fentanyl who enter OTPs may view the increased time needed to achieve an effective dose of methadone as evidence that methadone treatment will not work for them, and that this may serve as yet another barrier to treatment.

Current guidelines for methadone treatment by the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) recommend a maximum initial dose of 30 mg per federal OTP regulations, which were established before synthetic opioids became the leading cause of opioid-involved deaths in the United States. Guidelines state that the dose may be increased by 5 mg to 10 mg every 3 to 5 days. This dosing schedule may be ineffective for patients using fentanyl given their higher tolerance; it may take up to a month or more to reach an effective methadone dose in these patients.

The commentary authors offer several points to consider when adapting induction protocols to meet the therapeutic needs of patients using fentanyl and noted that change can be achieved without lengthy regulatory reform. The authors offer evidence from several US studies in which a more rapid methadone induction schedule allowed achievement of therapeutic doses more quickly without an increase in the risk for overdose, which is highest risk during the first few weeks of methadone induction in OTP settings.

This evidence indicates that OTP providers are attempting to address these concerns with a variety of induction variations, suggesting that more research focused on patients using fentanyl is needed.

This commentary is valuable in attempting to spur further innovative efforts to adapt the methadone OTP model to meet the challenges presented by the greater potency of fentanyl. Engagement early in induction can be challenging for any patient with opioid use disorder seeking treatment. Even before the rise in fentanyl use, many patients with opioid use disorder struggled with the induction period when they were initiated on doses that do little early on to suppress withdrawal symptoms, which are common. This problem is even greater now with the rise in fentanyl use, and this commentary demonstrates the need for OTPs to offer a model for how OTPs and OTP regulators can design more effective induction protocols that are both safe and effective.

This article originally appeared on Clinical Advisor

Buresh M, Nahvi S, Steiger S, Weinstein ZM. Adapting methadone inductions to the fentanyl era. J Subst Abuse Treat. 2022;141:108832. doi:10.1016/j.jsat.2022.108832

Psychiatry Advisor, a trusted source of medical news and feature content for healthcare providers, offers clinicians insight into the latest research to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes.

#9426. The Simple Drink Swap Linked To 41% More Weight Loss

Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

Women who changed their usual lunchtime drink lost 41 per cent more weight over 18 months. What made the difference?

Swapping diet drinks for water could help people lose more weight.

Women with type 2 diabetes who make the switch lose around 41 percent more weight over 18 months than those who continue drinking diet beverages.

They are also twice as likely to achieve diabetes remission during a structured weight-management programme.

The findings raise a question about whether a drink’s calorie count tells the whole story about its effects on weight.

Sweet taste without the accompanying energy might influence appetite signals.

The results suggest that everyday drink choices could play a useful supporting role in longer-term weight management.

The research involved around 80 women who were overweight or had obesity, had type 2 diabetes and regularly consumed diet drinks.

Researchers randomly assigned them either to replace their usual diet beverage with water after lunch five times a week or to continue drinking it.

Both groups took part in a six-month weight-loss programme followed by a year devoted to maintaining their progress.

By the end, women assigned to water had lost an average of 6.82 kg, compared with 4.85 kg among those continuing with diet drinks.

The difference amounted to almost 2 kg of additional weight loss across the programme.

The water group also showed greater improvements in measures including fasting blood glucose, insulin resistance and blood fats.

Diabetes remission was reported in 90 percent of women assigned to water, compared with 45 percent of those continuing diet beverages.

Dr Hamid R. Farshchi, study co-author, said:

“It’s a small change with the potential for a big impact on long-term health outcomes.”

The brain may respond differently when a sweet taste arrives without the energy normally supplied by sugar.

In a separate experiment involving around 75 adults, participants reported greater hunger after consuming sucralose than sugar, and the sweetener altered activity in the hypothalamus, a brain region involved in appetite regulation (Chakravartti et al., 2025).

However, hunger ratings after sucralose did not differ from those after water, so the findings do not establish that sweetened drinks necessarily make people hungrier than plain water.

The mismatch between sweetness and energy might help explain some appetite responses, but whether it contributed to the weight-loss difference remains unknown.

The study was published in the journal Diabetes (Farshchi Nasr et al., 2025).

#9424. AI anxiety: 5 ways to cope when you’re scared of AI

If you’re feeling a mix of emotions about artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and how they’re shaping our world, you’re not alone. Chief Clinical Officer at Calm, Chris Mosunic, PhD, has tips and strategies to help tame a growing source of anxiety.

AI anxiety is the worry or unease some people feel about the fast growth of artificial intelligence and how quickly technology is changing. It isn’t a clinical diagnosis, but the feelings are real and common. They can focus on everyday risks, such as job loss and AI-powered scams, and bigger ones, such as AI getting out of human control.

AI research goes back decades, but progress has sped up sharply in recent years with the arrival of chatbots, AI image generators, and other tools. A 2023 Calm survey* found that nearly 1 in 3 U.S. adults (29%) felt anxious about AI, and 18% described their feelings as fear or dread. At the same time, 31% felt optimistic, and 31% felt excited. Many respondents felt a mix: amazed by AI and nervous about it.

Concern about AI has stayed high in the years since. In a June 2026 Pew Research Center survey, 52% of U.S. adults said they feel more concerned than excited about AI in daily life. That’s up from 37% in 2021 and about the same as in 2023. Just 9% said they feel more excited than concerned.

It’s hard to know how AI will affect our safety and our lives. You might wonder how it will change your job, what it could mean for areas like scientific research, and what the future will look like. Many of us find uncertainty hard to cope with, so feeling anxious or out of control is understandable. But when anxiety feels overwhelming, it can start to affect your sleep, mood, and focus.

These five ways to manage AI anxiety draw on mindfulness and common thinking traps, like catastrophizing. Start with whichever fits how you feel today.

The rapid rise in AI and automation can feel like a threat to our livelihoods (and even our lives), making many of us feel unstable and out of control.

Resist resisting: When confronted with uncertainty, our first instinct can often be to fight it. Try sitting with it instead. Notice how the discomfort shows up in your body and mind.

Go at your own pace: Give yourself time to adjust to the new realities of AI.

Talk it out: Process your anxieties with a friend or a coworker. You may find someone who feels the same way.

💙 On those days when you feel overwhelmed by the rapidly changing tech landscape, try a simple meditation practice like Pause to Breathe to help you feel more grounded.

If you’re feeling anxious or uneasy about AI, don’t invalidate or try to avoid those emotions — that approach can make things worse. Instead, let yourself feel anxious. Telling yourself you’re overreacting can damage your self-trust and self-confidence.

Identify the emotions: Get a better understanding of what you’re feeling. Your anxiety could mean you’re working through a more deeply rooted problem, like feeling threatened or inadequate.

Try meditation: Meditation can help you ground yourself in the present moment and tune into what you’re feeling and where it’s coming from.

Write down all your anxieties without censoring yourself: Set aside dedicated time each day to think through your anxious thoughts, helping you process and make sense of your emotions.

💙 Take some time to stop and do this short Emotions Check-In to make space for any anxious feelings.

When we’re feeling anxious about the unknown, many of us fall into the trap of catastrophic thinking, imagining the worst possible outcome, even without evidence to support it. This can cause low-level anxieties to spiral out of control.

Challenge your worst fears: What evidence do you have that they’re true or that they’ll happen?

Bring to mind times in the past that felt groundbreaking in the tech world: Think back to the creation of mobile phones, laptops, or even navigation apps, and consider how you’ve adapted to their existence despite any initial anxieties or concerns. The same could happen with AI.

Bring your mind back to the now: The future feels a whole lot less intimidating when you focus on the present.

💙 One of the best ways you can bring yourself back to the present is through mindfulness meditation, which you can learn in the Mindfulness for Beginners series.

Many of us find ourselves viewing situations as an all-or-nothing approach. This is a cognitive distortion called polarized thinking, and it often occurs because we’re focused on the extremes without considering the nuances or possibilities of any given situation.

The debate around AI is nuanced. Popular culture shows dystopian futures, so it can be easy to think there’s only one possible outcome with AI.

However, reality tends to exist in between the extremes, so remind yourself that it’s perfectly normal for opposing emotions or views to be present at the same time. And they can also all feel as strong, real, or true as each other. You can feel fascinated and terrified, anxious and excited, or resentful and grateful.

When we allow multiple truths to co-exist in our minds, we make space for more ease. So try to hold space for the contradictions and the possibilities.

💙 For a more in-depth discussion on how to use mindfulness to combat worrying and keep nuance at the forefront, check out the Overcome Stress & Anxiety series.

At the extreme end of AI anxiety, some of us may have a deep—even subconscious—fear about a machine taking over. We ask questions like: Is this the beginning of the end of humanity? Will humans be replaced by robots?

A fear of overdependence on technology can cause us to worry about the negative consequences of relying too heavily on artificial intelligence. One way to remedy this fear is to embrace our humanity.

Be present for the little things you often take for granted, like hugs, laughing until it hurts, or exchanging a look with your best friend.

Make time for the people in your life, and prioritize connecting with them face-to-face when you can.

Marvel at the awesomeness of human things like awkward silences or goosebumps when you’re listening to music.

Ask people how they’re really feeling and practice deep listening when they respond.

Disconnect from technology and spend time in nature.

💙 Embrace the power of being human and living in the now by reading a book, listening to a meditation, or taking a Mindful Walk.

*Calm research was fielded among n = 450 adults in the US between March 21, 2023 and March 22, 2023 and is nationally representative, with quotas across age, gender, race, ethnicity, and region.

Recent news stories have shown how general-purpose AI tools may respond in unsafe or harmful ways, especially when people are vulnerable or struggling with a mental health crisis. These situations are rare, but they highlight an important truth: AI is not human and can’t accurately recognize risk, provide crisis support, or understand the complexity of your emotional world.

AI can support mental health — especially when it’s part of a program designed and guided by licensed professionals. But general AI tools, like chatbots or large language models, are not a replacement for real human care.

If you’re struggling, please consider reaching out to a therapist or support line — many offer free or low-cost options. You deserve support that’s personal, thoughtful, and real.

U.S. - Call or text 988 to reach the Suicide & Crisis Lifeline

Worldwide - Visit findahelpline.com for free, confidential resources

Your mental health matters and you don’t have to navigate tough moments alone.

To manage anxiety about artificial intelligence, there are proactive steps you can take.

Educate yourself about AI to understand its capabilities and limitations better: Learning about AI can make it feel less intimidating.

Engage in conversations about AI: Talking with others about your concerns can offer new perspectives and reduce feelings of isolation.

Practice mindfulness and stress-reduction techniques: Managing your anxiety effectively can help you focus on the present and reduce worries about the future.

Stay informed about AI developments: Understand how it's being integrated into society to help you feel more prepared and less anxious.

Understanding these fears and addressing them through education and dialogue can help alleviate the anxiety associated with AI.

You don’t have to be, though some concern is understandable. AI is changing fast, and it raises real questions, from job loss and scams to whether people can keep control of it. Some risks deserve attention. Others are far from certain, and no one knows exactly how AI will unfold. When we’re anxious, our minds jump to the worst outcome and can treat every headline as proof of a disastrous future.

It can help to follow reliable news sources and take breaks from stories that leave you on edge. When your thoughts race ahead, try a mindfulness practice to bring your attention back to today. If worry about AI is getting in the way of sleep or daily life, consider talking with a therapist or doctor.

The fear of AI doesn’t have a widely recognized specific term but is often considered a form of “technophobia,” which is the fear of advanced technology or complex devices. When this fear centers on AI, it can stem from concerns that the technology could surpass human intelligence and from the ethical consequences of machines making decisions that affect people’s lives. AI anxiety is rooted in the unknown future impact of AI on humanity.

On a societal level, increased reliance on AI could reduce human interaction and erode certain skills as machines take over more tasks. Understanding these potential negative effects can help develop strategies to mitigate them and ensure AI is used responsibly and ethically.

#9423. Increased Risk for Suicide Attempts Among Children Who Use Tobacco Products

Children who report the use of tobacco products — including e-cigarettes and vaping — have a 3 to 5 times increased risk for suicide attempts (SAs), according to study results published in JAMA Network Open.

New tobacco products (ie, e-cigarettes, vapes, hookahs) have become increasingly popular in the United States, particularly among children and adolescents. Although it is well-documented that adolescents and adults who smoke cigarettes have an increased likelihood of suicidality, it is unclear whether this heightened risk applies to children who use tobacco products.

To address this knowledge gap, researchers conducted a cross-sectional cohort study from September 1 to September 5, 2022. The researchers used data from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study, a nationally representative cohort of 11,868 US children enrolled at 9 and 10 years of age. The objective of the current study was to investigate the correlation between tobacco product use and the incidence of nonsuicidal self-injury (NSSI), suicidal ideation (SI), and SAs among preadolescent children. Substance use was evaluated using the ABCD Youth Substance Use Interview and hair toxicology tests at baseline, a 6-month follow-up, and then yearly. The researchers assessed suicidality using children and caregiver reports of the Kiddie Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia (K-SADS-5).

The researchers included data from 8988 children (median age, 9.8 years; 47.9% girls). At baseline, 1.1% of children reported ever using tobacco products, and this prevalence rose significantly to 1.7% at the 18-month follow-up. The researchers observed no statistical difference in smoking experience by sex or race/ethnicity; however, tobacco-using children generally came from more socioeconomically disadvantaged backgrounds, had greater prenatal smoking exposure, and were more likely to have parents with a history of depression, alcohol issues, and behavioral or suicide-related problems, relative to children who did not use tobacco products.

The researchers observed significant associations between tobacco product use among children and increased risks for SAs at each time point. Tobacco use was linked to a 3 to 5 times higher risk for SAs, with an odds ratio (OR) of 4.67 (95% CI, 2.35-9.27; P <.001) at baseline, 4.25 (95% CI, 2.33-7.74; P <.001) at 1 year, and 2.85 (95% CI, 1.58-5.12; P =.001) at year 2.

The researchers also evaluated whether children’s personality, cognition, and psychological outcomes were associated with tobacco product use. They found that children were more likely to endorse tobacco use if they had conduct disorder (P <.001), oppositional defiant disorder (P <.001), rule-breaking behaviors (P <.001), aggressive behaviors (P <.001), social problems (P =.009), attention problems (P =.02), as well as personality traits of lack of planning (P <.001), positive urgency (P =.006), lack of perseverance (P =.009), sensation seeking (P =.02), aggression (P =.02), negative urgency (P =.03), and depressive mood (P <.05).

However, the association between tobacco use and SAs remained elevated, independent of these behavioral/psychopathology traits (OR, 3.09; 95% CI, 1.70-5.65; P <.001) in regression analyses. Conversely, the association between tobacco use and SI was not sustained when childhood behavioral measures were considered.

Among other substance use, only alcohol sipping was independently associated with SAs (OR, 1.55; 95% CI, 1.14-2.13; P =.007). These findings suggest that while other substance use is related to SAs, tobacco product use remains a robust independent risk factor.

Study authors concluded, “The findings suggest that smoking tobacco products may be a modifiable risk factor that can be addressed in suicide prevention efforts, especially among children.”

These study findings may be limited by the use of hair toxicology tests to assess tobacco use and the inability to determine causality, given the observational study design.

Lee PH, Tervo-Clemmens B, Liu RT, et al. Use of tobacco products and suicide attempts among elementary school-aged children. JAMA Netw Open. Published online February 5, 2024. doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.0376

Psychiatry Advisor, a trusted source of medical news and feature content for healthcare providers, offers clinicians insight into the latest research to inform clinical practice and improve patient outcomes.
